item.title: Two frameworks advance zero-shot robot navigation capabilities
item.description:
Two frameworks advance zero-shot robot navigation capabilities

Recent research introduces two distinct frameworks addressing key challenges in zero-shot robot navigation: RPSI-Nav for recursive policy self-improvement in multi-object search, and ROMUX for navigation using uncalibrated exocentric cameras.

🧩 How RPSI-Nav Works

RPSI-Nav forms a recursive loop where the system revises both its navigation program and the revision mechanism itself:

  • Diagnoses search behavior and requests diagnostic views when observations cannot distinguish competing causes
  • Generates targeted navigation revisions based on diagnosis
  • Links feedback from subsequent goal searches to the rules that produced revisions
  • Updates the improver (diagnosis, observation acquisition, revision planning) to govern future improvements
  • Conditionally inherits accepted program updates and spatial memory across goals

🧩 How ROMUX Works

ROMUX predicts metric robot-centric obstacle maps from exocentric images without camera calibration:

  • Trains a cross-view transformer on large-scale simulation data to predict obstacle maps from exocentric images
  • Does not condition image tokens on camera information (pose or intrinsics)
  • Uses a small PPO-trained policy to navigate on predicted maps toward goal coordinates relative to the robot
  • Works with single or multiple cameras with partial views
  • Transfers zero-shot to real robots with cameras at varying positions and orientations across room layouts

⚙️ Key Details

Framework Task Key Innovation
RPSI-Nav Zero-shot open-vocabulary multi-object navigation Recursive self-improvement of both policy and improvement mechanism
ROMUX Point-goal navigation with obstacle avoidance Cross-view transformer predicting metric maps from uncalibrated, unknown exocentric cameras

💡 Why It Matters

  • RPSI-Nav addresses the constraint where fixed human-designed revision mechanisms limit continued self-improvement in navigation policies
  • ROMUX eliminates time-consuming calibration requiring specialized personnel, which must be repeated when cameras move or new rooms are navigated
  • Both systems operate zero-shot in unseen environments without training or fine-tuning
  • Benchmark experiments and real-robot evaluations validate both approaches
  • ROMUX matches success rates of policies using robot-mounted cameras in simulation with randomized cameras per episode

🚀 Availability

  • RPSI-Nav: Benchmark experiments and qualitative real-robot evaluations completed
  • ROMUX: Benchmarked in simulation with per-episode camera randomization; transferred zero-shot to real robot across various room layouts and camera positions/orientations

#robotics #navigation #zero-shot #embodied-ai #computer-vision #self-improvement

Source: Improve How You Improve: Recursive Policy Self-Improvement for Zero-Shot Open-Vocabulary Multi-Object Navigation Source: Navigating Robots from Unknown and Uncalibrated Exocentric Cameras via Map Estimation

item.title: Using Amazon Bedrock CloudWatch metrics and evals for LLM observability
item.description:
Using Amazon Bedrock CloudWatch metrics and evals for LLM observability

Airbnb uses Amazon Bedrock to run its internal coding agent tool, AirChat, and has developed a specific observability workflow that combines AWS CloudWatch metrics with custom evaluations. This approach allows the engineering team to monitor production performance, manage costs, and validate model changes effectively.

🔍 Overview

Amazon Bedrock provides access to foundation models from multiple providers through a common API, with AWS managing the underlying infrastructure. At Airbnb, thousands of engineers use AirChat weekly to run coding agents. These agents send model requests through an internal LLM gateway that runs on Amazon Bedrock, ensuring that Airbnb’s code, prompts, and model responses are processed within AWS. The system integrates with standard AWS access controls and monitoring tools.

⚙️ Key Details

To manage the impact of frequent model updates, Airbnb utilizes a combination of operational metrics and quality evaluations:

  • Evaluations (Evals): Before a new model rollout, the team runs evals on a fixed set of representative tasks to measure the model’s score and cost per task.
  • Production Observability: After a rollout, observability data is used to compare production usage against eval results. If discrepancies exist, the team investigates the cause.
  • Cost Per Task: This is defined as the list-price cost of all tokens an agent uses to finish one task. It serves as a key metric alongside performance scores to determine default model and reasoning effort settings.

CloudWatch Metrics for Bedrock

Most production problems can be diagnosed using specific signals in the AWS/Bedrock namespace in CloudWatch. The following table outlines the key metrics used to monitor latency, throttling, and cost:

Category Metric Description
Latency InvocationLatency Measures time from API call to response.
Latency TimeToFirstToken Time until the first token is generated.
Latency OutputTokenCount Total output tokens generated.
Latency OTPS Output tokens per second (derived metric).
Throttling InvocationThrottles Count of throttled requests.
Throttling EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage Estimated tokens per minute quota consumption, including cache write tokens and output burndown multipliers, across inference APIs.
Cost InputTokenCount Uncached input tokens.
Cost CacheReadInputTokenCount Input tokens read from cache (lower cost than uncached).
Cost CacheWriteInputTokenCount Input tokens written to cache (can have higher cost depending on model).
Cost OutputTokenCount Generated output tokens.

The EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage metric helps teams set proactive alarms, track quota consumption across models, and request quota increases before hitting rate limits. A lower cache hit rate can increase the cost per request due to the pricing differences between uncached input and cache reads.

💡 Why It Matters

In a period of about five weeks, eight new models were released. By mid-October, approximately two-thirds of engineer requests through coding agents were directed to these new models. Each release can simultaneously change output tokens, cost, latency, and capacity. Since published benchmark charts do not always reflect how a model handles specific internal workloads, Airbnb’s approach of running evals on their own tasks and monitoring distinct CloudWatch signals allows them to choose appropriate default models and reasoning effort ceilings for their engineers.

#AmazonBedrock #CloudWatch #LLMObservability #Airbnb #AIEngineering

Source: How Airbnb uses cost per task to operate coding agents on Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services

item.title: A2A Java SDK releases client and server support for agent communication

A new Java library has been released to support the execution of agentic applications as Agent2Agent (A2A) servers. This multi-module Maven library provides both client and server capabilities, enabling A2A agent communication across JSON-RPC, gRPC, and REST transports.

The library facilitates agent-to-agent interaction by implementing the A2A Protocol. For gRPC support, the project copies the a2a.proto file from the A2A specification repository into the spec-grpc/ project. The java_package option is adjusted to target the org.a2aproject.sdk.grpc package. Developers can regenerate the gRPC classes by building the module with the command mvn clean install -Dskip.protobuf.generate=false.

  • Language Requirement: Java 17 or later is required.
  • Transport Protocols: Supports JSON-RPC, gRPC, and REST.

🚀 Availability and Integrations

Developers can add the A2A Java SDK reference server for JSON-RPC to their Maven projects. The SDK includes examples for cross-language integration, such as a Java A2A server communicating with a Python client, and a Java A2A client communicating with a Python server.

    • agent-shell-bookmark: Bookmark support for agent-shell sessions.

    • agent-shell-manager: Tabulated view and management of agent-shell buffers.
    • agent-review: Code review interface for agent-shell.
    • agent-shell-attention.el: Mode-line attention tracker for agent-shell.
    • agent-shell-knockknock: Notifications for agent-shell via knockknock.el.
    • agent-shell-notifications: Desktop notifications for agent-shell events.
    • meta-agent-shell: Multi-agent coordination system for agent-shell with inter-agent communication, task tracking, and project-level dispatching.

⚙️ Key details

  • Run thousands of AI agent sandboxes on the cheapest machines.
  • Sandstorm pauses idle sandboxes and snapshots them to disk, then restores them quickly when a request arrives, so one machine can hold far more sandboxes than it could run at once.
  • It supports two sandbox backends, gVisor containers and Firecracker microVMs.
  • Every sandbox has its own network namespace, and both backends can run in one fleet, each forming a resource pool of its own.
  • The master serves a web console for viewing and managing sandboxes and scheduling across the fleet.
  • Agents spend much of their time waiting.
  • Sandstorm is designed around this behavior, with four sandbox tiers that progressively suspend idle sandboxes and quickly wake them when requests arrive.
  • The master keeps desired state in SQLite and places sandboxes.
  • Nodes join by address and pairing code, or dial out from behind NAT.
  • A gateway on the sandbox’s node wakes it and forwards the request.
  • Nodes refuse new work when memory runs low, so SSH stays reachable.
  • sandstormd serves as the master, node, and web console.
  • gVisor and Firecracker each get their own optimizations.
  • The master’s web console shows sandbox states, tier transitions, and node headroom.
  • Measured 2026-10-31, with requests from each node to its own gateway, so no network is in the path.
  • gVisor needs no KVM and ran on six cloud nodes.
  • Firecracker ran on one machine with KVM and one cloud VM under PVM.
  • The hosts differ, so read each column on its own.
  • Traffic is 40 sandboxes per node with a few getting most requests; about 12 fit awake on a gVisor node.
  • p50 is 6-10 ms on gVisor, 7-50 ms on KVM.

🚀 Availability

  • agent-shell is available with additional packages to extend its functionality.

💡 Why it matters

  • agent-shell brings AI agents to Emacs, providing a familiar and integrated environment for AI interactions.
  • The use of ACP allows for compatibility with a wide range of AI agents.
  • The sandboxing and management features of Sandstorm enable efficient and scalable AI agent operations.

#AIagents #Emacs #ACP #Sandstorm #agent-shell

Source: xenodium/agent-shell Source: deeplethe/sandstorm

item.title: ATLAS-Finance Benchmark Tests AI Agents in Complex Banking Tasks
item.description:
ATLAS-Finance Benchmark Tests AI Agents in Complex Banking Tasks

🔍 Overview

Researchers introduced ATLAS-Finance, a benchmark designed to evaluate how well frontier AI agents can perform realistic banking tasks. These tasks mirror the challenges of professional work—where information is fragmented across emails, files, and tools—and require agents to reconcile conflicting data and build financial models. The benchmark assesses 100 investment-banking tasks across 13 simulated firms, developed by experienced bankers based on real-world workflows.

🧩 How it works

  • Task Design: Each task mimics the complexity of real banking assignments, taking 15–30 hours for human professionals to complete.
  • Data Sources: Agents must search emails, chats, calendars, notes, and files to identify requirements and gather information.
  • Evaluation Criteria: Deliverables are judged by expert rubrics covering financial rationale, spreadsheet construction, completeness, and formatting (median: 124.5 criteria).
  • Current Performance: Despite partial task completion, no frontier AI agent (including Claude Opus and Fable) passes fewer than 11% of tasks.

⚙️ Key details

  • Benchmark Scope: 100 end-to-end investment-banking tasks across 13 simulated firms.
  • Agent Models Tested: Claude Opus and Fable (performance metrics not explicitly detailed beyond passing <11% of tasks).
  • Evaluation Method: Expert-authored rubrics with 124.5+ criteria per task.

🚀 Availability

The research paper is available for download via:

  • View PDF (Note: Replace placeholder URL with actual source if available; evidence does not specify a direct link.)

💡 Why it matters

ATLAS-Finance highlights the persistent gap between AI agents’ capabilities and the demands of professional, real-world workflows. By exposing how poorly current models handle fragmented, dynamic data—key to banking—it sets a critical benchmark for future advancements in AI-driven financial automation.

item.title: AWS Agent Registry Introduces Custom Metadata Schemas for Structured Governance
item.description:
AWS Agent Registry Introduces Custom Metadata Schemas for Structured Governance

Custom metadata schemas are now available in AWS Agent Registry. This update allows administrators to define a set of organization-specific key-value pairs that registry records must carry, enabling structured validation, discovery, and governance.

🔍 Overview

AWS Agent Registry provides a catalog to register, approve, and discover resources and custom records. Each record within the registry carries a name, a description, a protocol descriptor, and an approval status. With the introduction of custom metadata schemas, administrators can enforce structured metadata on every record to maintain consistency across teams.

⚙️ How it works

A custom metadata schema is a set of organization-defined key-value pairs. The registry administrator defines the schema—including field names, types, allowed values, and whether each field is required or optional—and applies it to the registry.

Key behaviors of the schema validation include:

  • Supported Field Types: Each field can be configured as Text, Enum, URL, or Boolean.
  • Scope of Fields: The schema has common attributes that apply to every record type, and administrators can add dedicated fields that only apply to specific record types.
  • Enforcement and Validation: When a record is created or updated, AWS Agent Registry validates the custom metadata against the schema. If a record includes an unknown field, a missing required field, or an invalid value, it is rejected with a ValidationException.
  • Compliance Status: If a record is created without any custom metadata, AWS Agent Registry saves it as NON_COMPLIANT. Calling GetRegistryRecord returns the record’s custom metadata values and its compliance status.

🧩 Supported Fields and Enrichment

Organizations can use custom metadata fields to track ownership, environments, and compliance. Examples of these fields include:

  • Environment & Ownership: Fields such as environment (prod, staging, or dev), businessUnit, ownerTeam, supportContact, and costCenter record where a resource runs, who is responsible for it, and who pays for it.
  • Inventory Integration: A configuration management database (CMDB) ID links the record to an existing inventory, and a support-tier field sets expectations for dependents.
  • Security & Compliance: Fields such as data classification, compliance scope (like PCI or HIPAA), risk tier, scan status, and a scan report URL turn approvals into reviews of structured evidence. Existing scanners, CMDB sync jobs, and classification tools can write these values through the API before a record is submitted.

🔍 Discovery and Filtering

Custom metadata values are indexed for search. Approvers can use the validated values when reviewing records, and consumers and agents can use Discovery APIs to filter records based on custom attributes.

For example, a consumer or agent can combine a natural-language query with specific metadata filters, such as:

1

environment=prod AND businessUnit=payments AND securityScanStatus=PASSED

To ensure security, only approved records are returned; a record that matches the filters but has not been approved is omitted from the results.

As a use case, AnyCompany operates anycompany-governed-registry without auto-approval. Its payments team publishes an MCP record, payments-ledger-mcp (a read-only server for ledger lookups). Existing security and inventory systems enrich this MCP record before an approval function determines whether consumers can discover it.

🚀 Prerequisites

To get started with custom metadata schemas, you need:

  • An AWS account in a supported AWS Region.
  • Python 3.11 or later.
  • boto3 1.43.113 or later.

#AWSAgentRegistry #CloudGovernance #MetadataSchemas #CloudSecurity

Source: Govern and discover records with common metadata in AWS Agent Registry | Amazon Web Services

item.title: AWS Expands Forward Deployed Engineering to 15 Countries to Scale Enterprise Agents
item.description:
AWS Expands Forward Deployed Engineering to 15 Countries to Scale Enterprise Agents

AWS has expanded its AWS Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) service to 15 countries, providing commercial and public sector customers with built-in, production-ready accelerators to deploy secure, governed agentic AI. Launched in June, FDE helps organizations establish the necessary foundations—including identity, security, context, governance, and operational controls—required to scale agents across high-volume, rule-heavy processes.

🚀 Global Expansion

AWS FDE is now available for commercial and public sector customers in 15 countries:

  • United States
  • Mexico
  • Brazil
  • Canada
  • Australia
  • Singapore
  • India
  • South Korea
  • Japan
  • United Kingdom
  • Germany
  • Netherlands
  • France
  • Sweden
  • Saudi Arabia

🔍 Overcoming Foundational AI Gaps

Before an AI agent can perform useful work at scale, it requires a secure foundation. Many organizations struggle because their data is spread across different systems without a common ontology—the shared model of how the business works. Without this foundation, the cost of consecutive pilots remains high. AWS FDE addresses these challenges by ensuring each agent receives its own distinct identity, permissions, and audit trail, separate from human identity.

⚙️ Standardizing Work with AWS Quick

AWS Quick provides an AI workspace built for work, allowing teams to share dashboards, agents, and automations. Designed with enterprise-grade security, it connects to everyday systems while offering:

  • Tenant-level data isolation to separate distinct user populations or competing dealers.
  • Role-based access controls to enforce fine-grained permissions by business function.
  • Structured approval workflows for agentic actions and protection of confidential information.
  • Automated audit frameworks to prove compliance to regulators and internal standards.

📊 Real-World Implementations

Customer Core Challenge Solution and Action Outcome Timeline
Samsung Life Insurance Four affiliates each building separate AI point solutions from scratch. FDE team built a governed agentic platform with a single control plane. Completed in 45 days; new agents register instead of being rebuilt.
Rio Tinto Iron Ore Supply chain running on a 30-year-old Oracle system with 5,000+ tables and 140 apps. FDE team built agents to map system dependencies for teams to validate. Mapped in weeks
Marsh Needed agent security controls that hold up under strict audit standards. FDE team integrated permissions, identities, and audit trails. Reached production in about two months
Allianz Needed to empower 200,000 employees across regulated markets while meeting compliance. Deployed AWS Quick with structured approval workflows and custom branding. Moved from evaluation to “go” in six weeks

#AWS #AIagents #EnterpriseAI #CloudComputing

item.title: Curated Catalog of Open-Source MLSecOps Tools for AI Security
item.description:
Curated Catalog of Open-Source MLSecOps Tools for AI Security

A new curated catalog has been released to help security engineers, machine learning practitioners, developers, and AI red teams discover resources for integrating security into the machine learning lifecycle.

🔍 Overview

MLSecOps (Machine Learning Security Operations) is the practice of integrating security throughout the machine learning lifecycle, spanning data collection, model development, deployment, monitoring, and incident response. This catalog compiles open-source tools, adversarial machine learning research, AI security frameworks, threat-modeling resources, and practical learning materials to support these efforts.

🧩 How it works

The catalog applies security testing, threat modeling, supply-chain protection, access controls, and continuous monitoring to machine learning models, MLOps pipelines, LLM applications, and AI agents. The resources are organized into specific functional categories:

Category Function
Model and artifact security tools Detect unsafe serialization, malicious payloads, integrity failures, and other risks in machine learning model files.
Adversarial machine learning testing tools Evaluate model robustness against evasion, poisoning, extraction, inversion, and other adversarial techniques.
Embodied AI and robotics ML security tools Test policies that emit actions rather than text, where a successful attack moves a robot out of its safe envelope rather than changing a prediction.

💡 Why it matters

Open-source MLSecOps tools allow practitioners to test, monitor, and protect machine learning models, data, pipelines, LLM applications, and AI agents. The catalog serves as a central discovery point for these resources, including active projects and proofs of concept.

⚙️ Key details

  • The collection includes a mix of active projects and proofs of concept.
  • Users are advised to evaluate maintenance status, licensing, threat coverage, and deployment suitability before production use.
  • The newsletter for the MLSecOps Hacker focuses on model supply-chain security (serialization, signing, provenance), prompt injection, and agent and MCP security.

#MLSecOps #AISecurity #MLOps #OpenSource #ThreatModeling

item.title: DVLAA launches local security range for LLM and agent training
item.description:
DVLAA launches local security range for LLM and agent training

DVLAA (Damn Vulnerable LLM and Agent Application) is a localized security range platform for testing, educational drills, and defense verification of large language model (LLM) and agent applications. The project centers on the OWASP LLM Top 10 and Agent Application Security Top 10 risk frameworks, covering typical scenarios such as prompt injection, sensitive information leakage, RAG poisoning, tool abuse, permission boundaries, memory contamination, output processing, and resource consumption.

🔍 Overview

The platform operates as a unified training environment that integrates theoretical vulnerability introductions, interactive answering pages, and state-machine verification. It is designed as a “theory-first” entry structure, where users first review vulnerability definitions, attack surfaces, and risk boundaries before proceeding to interactive challenges. The system builds a complete training loop: from vulnerability introduction to answering, model/state machine interaction, audit panels, flag verification, and write-ups (WP).

🧩 How it works

DVLAA uses a Flask console as its main entry point, organizing capabilities into a monolithic Flask application with lightweight sidecar containers. The system validates payloads through real model responses, tool calls, state machines, or multi-turn context progression, rather than relying on hardcoded frontend rules.

  • LLM Focus: Emphasizes risks in prompts, context, RAG, output processing, tool calls, and resource consumption.
  • Agent Focus: Emphasizes goal hijacking, tool abuse, identity/permissions, supply chain, code execution, memory contamination, multi-agent communication, cascade failures, human-machine trust, and runaway agents.
  • Question Formats: Includes chat terminals, business command workspaces, product simulation skins, and read-only material workspaces depending on the track.

⚙️ Key details

The platform includes 81 local training questions, structured as follows:

Question Type Count Description
OWASP LLM Sub-questions 24 Derived from the LLM Top 10 framework
Agent Scenarios 10 Derived from the Agent Security Top 10 framework
Comprehensive Attack/Defense 11 Integrated scenarios
AWDP Attack/Defense Contest 30 Contest-based questions
Real Contest Adaptations 6 LLM poisoning CTFs adapted from real contests

Key features include:

  • Source Code & Prompt Viewer: Users can view system prompts, runtime configurations, and core implementations on question pages; runtime random flags are replaced with placeholders.
  • Model Management Backend: Supports configuration for local models, Ollama, SiliconFlow, and OpenAI-Compatible services, with API key masking and connection testing.
  • AWDP Dual-Track Environment: Offers a default product simulation track (no official image pull required) and an option to install and start official containers (Dify, RAGFlow, Langflow, Flowise, Open WebUI, n8n) for real reproduction.
  • Bilingual & Theme Support: Top navigation allows toggling between dark/light themes and Chinese/English interfaces, with preferences saved locally in the browser.
  • Learning Resources: Provides built-in Chinese study materials, Markdown/PDF upload, online reading, and material classification management.

🚀 Availability

DVLAA is available for local execution via direct Python running or Docker image deployment to independent containers. All vulnerability environments are exposed through a single gateway port (5080). Runtime data isolation ensures that model configurations, uploaded materials, and downloaded models are stored in runtime directories or Docker data volumes. An online AI security training entry point has been integrated with Prompt Airlines, providing a five-level Chinese question guide, stable WPs, and system-internal transfer for real interaction.

#LLMSecurity #AIAgents #CTF #OWASP #Flask #Docker

item.title: Five new developments in long-term AI memory and agent evolution
item.description:
Five new developments in long-term AI memory and agent evolution

Recent technical updates in artificial intelligence focus on improving how agents manage long-term memory, evolve their internal states, and handle stale data or corrupted inputs. These developments span architectural innovations for memory storage, learnable policies for memory transformation, governance strategies for conflicting facts, and the impact of data corruption on recall accuracy.

🔍 Overview of Memory Innovations

  • KV-LTM: A new memory tier stores raw session text plus the KV cache under a fixed reader model, answering queries by restoring cached sessions.
  • EvoDisco: Formulates agent memory evolution as evolutionary strategy discovery, allowing agents to learn which operators to apply rather than following a static schedule.
  • RegimeCouncil: An online router that arbitrates between local and global memory sharing scopes to manage stale facts without retraining the LLM.
  • Corrupted Memory Testing: A study testing whether intentionally corrupting training data prevents LLM agents from overfitting to recent events.

🧩 How It Works

KV-LTM Architecture This approach is complementary to retrieval and indexing. It treats text as the memory of record while using the cache as a recompute-free prefill accelerator. The design includes:

  • Storage records and budget-derived retention.
  • An append-only read path and bounded aggregation.
  • Analytical sizing where per-token state spans approximately 31K-328K bytes for pinned BF16 full-attention and latent-cached MLA configurations.
  • A per-user-year storage estimate of approximately 0.34-3.6 TB at a 30K-token/day scenario, compared to approximately 49 MB of raw text.

EvoDisco Policy A learnable policy conditions on current memory state and recent task history to select and instantiate one of four semantic operators:

Operator Function
Abstract Compress related memories
Refine Decompose overloaded entries
Bridge Connect weakly linked experiences
Reframe Reorganize retrieved reasoning chains

The policy updates via a bi-level fitness: an inner signal scores transformation quality, while an outer signal scores strategic efficacy over past decisions.

RegimeCouncil Governance This system addresses the “memory conflict governance” problem where stored facts go stale. It uses a paired-evidence router with three modules:

  • Local Advisor: Tracks the latest outcome on a queried fact alone.
  • Global Advisor: Pools recent outcomes across all stored facts.
  • Meta Governor: Defaults to the Local Advisor to avoid cross-fact interference but switches to the Global Advisor when global pooling shows a positive utility margin.

⚙️ Key Details and Results

  • KV-LTM Evaluation: Requires no persistent-cache implementation for logical QA evaluation. It uses per-session prefill to emulate valid cache reuse. System-level comparisons on LongMemEval indicate that commercial assistants often score below models reading history offline, consistent with content loss between write and read phases.
  • EvoDisco Performance: In a one-pass online plus frozen-transfer protocol on ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench, EvoDisco outperforms strong memory baselines like MemP and MemRL. The largest gains are observed on ALFWorld, with improvements of +8.8 to +12.9 points over MemP and +16.4 to +17.9 points over MemRL.
  • RegimeCouncil Performance: Across LongMemEval update streams and historical drift tests on TempLAMA and TAQA, RegimeCouncil outperforms the better fixed-scope policy by 5.2-7.3 points on primary disagreement episodes. Ablations show that removing any of its three modules reduces accuracy by 2-7 points.
  • Dream Hypothesis Test: An agent using Claude Opus 5.5 stored learned information in text memory and rewrote it nightly from transcripts with 5-40% corruption. The results showed that corruption did not help the agent apply earlier learned tasks. Replacing details in 40% of turns lowered recall from 76% to 60%. Random-text corruption had no consistent effect because the model recognized it as corrupted and excluded it from memory.

💡 Why It Matters

These updates address critical inefficiencies in long-term AI interactions. KV-LTM trades storage for avoided re-prefill compute and write-time fidelity, solving the problem where personal assistants accumulate months of conversations but struggle with derivation and selection. EvoDisco moves beyond fixed memory operators, allowing agents to dynamically decide how to transform their memory based on strategic efficacy. RegimeCouncil provides a lightweight method to handle delayed feedback from stale facts without the complexity of full LLM retraining. Finally, the corruption testing suggests that pretrained models can easily separate corrupted text from real events, implying that fair tests of memory evolution require learners that cannot make this distinction as easily, such as those fine-tuned on specific corrupted data or operating in invented worlds.

#AIMemory #LLMAgents #KVCache #AIResearch #LongTermMemory

Source: KV-LTM: Persistent Per-Session KV Caches as Long-Term Memory for Personal Assistants Source: EvoDisco: Strategy Discovery for Evolving Agent Memory Source: RegimeCouncil: Paired-Evidence Routing For Memory Conflict Governance In LLM Agents Source: Can an LLM dream? Testing the overfitted brain hypothesis on an agent with text memory

item.title: GitHub develops Agent Host Protocol to enable continuous multi-device AI sessions
item.description:
GitHub develops Agent Host Protocol to enable continuous multi-device AI sessions

The newly developed Agent Host Protocol (AHP) is an open standard designed to keep AI agent sessions accessible and continuous across editors, applications, mobile phones, and the cloud. As models become capable of working independently for hours or days, AHP ensures that developers can check in on their progress from any device, allowing sessions to persist even when users switch devices or close windows.

🔍 Overview

In the past, GitHub Copilot was built as a VS Code extension, tying the lifetime of agents directly to the VS Code editor window. Closing the window, restarting VS Code for an update, or connecting to a remote machine would terminate the agent session or reset the extension host. To resolve this limitation and allow developers to pull agents into their custom workflows, editors, terminals, or mobile apps, the Agent Host Protocol provides a standard, independently versioned language. This shared protocol ensures every client sees the same agents, history, and state without requiring bespoke, one-off integrations.

🧩 How it works

To handle multi-client interactions seamlessly, the Agent Host Protocol is designed with several core architectural features:

  • URI-identified Channels: This is the coarsest unit of functionality in the protocol. Every server must implement the root, session, and chat channels, and can optionally implement other channels such as terminal support, Model Context Protocol (MCP) additions, or OpenTelemetry (OTel) reporting.
  • Reducer-Based State Object: Inside each channel, a reducer-based state object drives client-side logic. The server acts as the arbiter of this state, while the client sends a sequence of actions that either mutate the state or trigger side effects.
  • Network Resiliency: Under poor network conditions, reconnection and replay are simplified. Clients can send all queued actions and present a loading state while waiting for the server to reconcile and acknowledge the actions.
  • Minimal Core: To make implementation straightforward on custom clients and servers, the core protocol is kept minimal while allowing extensive features to be built on top.

⚙️ Key details

  • Focus on Interaction, Not Behavior: Unlike the Language Server Protocol (LSP) or Debug Adapter Protocol (DAP), AHP avoids encoding how agents work, focusing solely on how users interact with them to accommodate rapidly evolving agent models.
  • Rebuilding the VS Code Stack: Adopting AHP in VS Code required building a new harness and agentic stack underneath it. The existing Copilot Chat extension had grown for over three years to more than 400,000 lines of TypeScript (excluding tests) and was heavily dependent on the VS Code window lifecycle and APIs that are unavailable in a standalone agent host process.

#AHP #GitHubCopilot #AIAgents #VSCode #DeveloperTools

Source: Building the Agent Host Protocol for sessions that continue across devices

item.title: Introducing the External Sandbox Pattern for Secure AI Agent Code Execution
item.description:
Introducing the External Sandbox Pattern for Secure AI Agent Code Execution

On November 17, 2026, a new project developed in collaboration with Prime Radiant introduced the external sandbox pattern. Under this pattern, code executed by an AI agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox, while the agent itself resides outside of that sandbox.

🔍 Overview

The external sandbox pattern separates the AI agent from the environment where its executed code runs. To demonstrate this pattern, three sandbox server implementations have been released. These sandboxes can be configured to receive API calls from AI agents such as Pi, Claude Code, or Codex whenever they need to execute code.

⚙️ Key features

  • Unified API: Each implementation offers the same localhost API.
  • Allow-list Proxy: An optional HTTP/HTTPS proxy to control exactly which hosts the agent’s code is allowed to communicate with.
  • Credential Replacement: A mechanism that allows the agent’s code to make authenticated API calls without sharing secret credentials directly with the agent.

🧩 Sandbox implementations

Implementation Description
external-sandbox-v86 A Node.js server that uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly.
external-sandbox-container A Python web server that runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance.
external-sandbox-quicksand A Python web server that uses Microsoft’s Quicksand sandboxing library to bundle QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package.

#AIAgents #Sandboxing #PrimeRadiant #SecureCode

Source: External sandboxes for coding agents

item.title: Mini-AGI: Continual Learning Model Trained on 8GB VRAM Laptop
item.description:
Mini-AGI: Continual Learning Model Trained on 8GB VRAM Laptop

A new continual learning byte-level language model, mini-AGI, has been trained from scratch on a single 8GB VRAM GPU. This model, which stores its weights as ordinary files on disk, can grow new capacity while training and prune what it doesn’t need. It is targeted at a PC or laptop with at least a 6GB VRAM GPU on the board.

🔍 Overview

  • mini-AGI is a continual learning byte-level language model that assembles its own architecture.
  • It trains from scratch on a single 8GB VRAM GPU and keeps learning from everything it reads.
  • The model stores its weights as ordinary files on disk and pages them onto the card as it needs them.
  • The parameter count is bounded by free disk space rather than by VRAM.
  • It grows new capacity while training when it runs short, prunes what nothing asks for, and reads through exactly the same code path it serves on.

⚙️ Key details

  • The model is pointed to the corpus to constantly read and learn from.
  • History - here is the samples from the whole training run history so far.
  • You can inspect them yourself to see how the model improved over the course of training/reading the corpus.
  • The model is rather a small experiment to show that continual learning from the single stream of data without catastrophic forgetting is possible.
  • Furthermore, it is possible on a modest hardware.
  • The capabilities would be bounded by the actual hardware, scale, and quality of the data available and the amount of time one willing to spend on training the model.

🚀 Availability

  • The “final” weights are not published yet.
  • The run is still reading its first pass over the corpus, the weights go up once it has been through all of it, which is several weeks away at the current rate.
  • If you would like to play with undertrained weights as they are right now, you can find the most recent (9 Nov 2026) snapshot here: https://huggingface.co/Volotat/mini-AGI-undertrained/tree/main

💡 Why it matters

  • Continual single-stream learning and natural size and processing adaptation to the available resources exactly what I myself expect from an AGI to have.
  • It has just a small toy-level memory footprint and hence it is “mini-AGI”.
  • The name is a half-joke and not a statement of the current capabilities of the model, but rather the potential and traits it has.
  • This is rather a small experiment to show, that continual learning from the single stream of data without catastrophic forgetting is possible.
  • Furthermore, it is possible on a modest hardware.
  • Which means that almost everyone could train their own version of the model (or simply continue training this one) exactly as they see it fit.

#AI #MachineLearning #ContinualLearning #miniAGI #LanguageModel

Source: volotat/mini-AGI

item.title: Nvidia’s Vera Rubin AI Chips Drive Record Data Center Growth and Frontier Model Adoption
item.description:
Nvidia’s Vera Rubin AI Chips Drive Record Data Center Growth and Frontier Model Adoption

🔍 Overview

Nvidia’s Vera Rubin NVL72 AI computing system has generated $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production, marking the fastest product ramp in the company’s history. The platform’s deployment by major tech firms—including CoreWeave, Google, Microsoft, and Oracle—has accelerated adoption of frontier AI models, with companies like OpenAI and Anthropic expanding access to its capacity through cloud providers. Nvidia’s revenue surged 110% year-over-year in Q3, while AMD reported record growth in data center sales, driven by high-end AI workloads.

🧩 How it works

The Vera Rubin NVL72 is designed for both training and inference of large AI models, including those used by AI agents. Nvidia’s latest earnings call highlighted its positioning for frontier labs, with expectations that these models will account for ~15% of its data center revenue this fiscal year. The system integrates with Nvidia’s existing ecosystem, including cloud partnerships and AMD’s Helios high-end GPUs for similar workloads.

The rapid adoption of frontier AI models—driven by Nvidia’s Vera Rubin NVL72 and AMD’s Helios systems—has reshaped data center spending. With token usage surging and GPU rental prices rising, companies are prioritizing high-performance AI infrastructure. Nvidia’s dominance in AI computing is further cemented as major labs adopt its chips, while AMD competes with its own high-end offerings. item.title: Output-Side Compression Model Achieves High Code Fidelity and Low Token Usage
item.description:
Output-Side Compression Model Achieves High Code Fidelity and Low Token Usage

A new development in output-side compression has been released. It achieves high code fidelity while reducing token usage significantly.

🔍 Overview

The development is described as “Brain big. Mouth small.” It is measured against reference answers, not base Gemma. The entire project cost under five dollars and fifty minutes of GPU time.

🧩 How it works

The system takes 185 tokens in and outputs 56. It preserves meaning at 0.91–0.98 cosine. It works by answering questions with about a quarter fewer tokens than verbose reference answers.

⚙️ Key details

  • Code Fidelity: Code fences are reproduced byte-exact 96–100% of the time. Identifiers, error strings, CLI commands, and code never move.
  • Configuration: It requires no skill file, no system prompt, and no /caveman toggle.
  • Variants: There are two flavors, selected by VRAM.
  • Metrics: Every number mentioned falls out of eval/metrics.py.

🚀 Availability

You can rebuild it today. It reaches places a system prompt cannot, such as embedded hosts, third-party agent frameworks, and any environment that owns its own prompt template.

#AI #MachineLearning #CodeGeneration #Optimization

Source: JuliusBrussee/cavegemma

item.title: Pupavision: AI-powered instrument for fruit fly pupariation monitoring
item.description:
Pupavision: AI-powered instrument for fruit fly pupariation monitoring

Pupavision is a low-cost, AI-powered instrument designed to monitor and record pupariation in fruit flies, addressing limitations in biology experiments.

🔍 Overview

  • Pupavision is a small physical AI instrument built from a single-board Linux computer and a day/night camera.
  • It is designed to monitor the timing of pupariation in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, providing biologically relevant information about growth regulation.

🧩 How it works

  • A frontier coding agent runs its agentic harness directly on the tiny board.
  • The model thinks in the cloud, but the agent works on the device.
  • The agent assists image capture, writes code to repair errors, and checks the experiment every day to keep raw data capture reliable.
  • If recording stops, the researcher gets a ping on their mobile phone.
  • A simple deterministic capture service records one image every ten minutes and never depends on the agent.

⚙️ Key details

  • Pupavision offers a blueprint for do-it-yourself agentic instruments that put frontier intelligence on a tiny board, with deterministic code underneath.
  • It is built for roughly 45 to 75 US dollars in parts.
  • A researcher-in-the-loop workflow then produces per-vial pupariation curves by tracing selected pupae backward in time from a late reference frame.

🚀 Availability

  • Pupavision is presented as an early case study from a pilot lab deployment.
  • It was tested for 26 days in a fly incubator, including eleven days in which the agent was logged out and capture continued, and a 51-hour outage.

💡 Why it matters

  • Pupavision contributes lessons learned toward a future where scientific domain experts are empowered by DIY agentic hardware.
  • Future work will validate the assay for lifecycle tracking accuracy against expert-labeled data and expand real-time computer vision analysis.

📚 arXivLabs

  • arXivLabs is a framework that allows collaborators to develop and share new arXiv features directly on their website.
  • arXiv is committed to values of openness, community, excellence, and user data privacy.
  • arXiv only works with partners that adhere to these values.

#Pupavision #AIinstrument #fruitfly #biology #AIagents

Source: Big Brains, Tiny Board: Pupavision, an Agentic Physical AI Instrument for Monitoring Drosophila Pupariation and Lifecycle Transitions

item.title: Readie Uses Learned Snapshots to Speed Up AI Agent Code Sandboxes
item.description:
Readie Uses Learned Snapshots to Speed Up AI Agent Code Sandboxes

Researchers have introduced Readie, a system that applies learned startup snapshots to reduce latency in code sandboxes used by AI agents for iterative code generation and execution.

🔍 Overview

  • AI agents act by iteratively generating and executing code for tasks ranging from quantitative research to personal assistance
  • Many agents offload execution to dedicated code sandboxes to decouple the agent harness from code execution
  • Existing code sandboxes suffer from slow startup because it is hard to build a compact, pre-warmed snapshot that covers nearly all required artifacts (packages, datasets) across diverse agent-generated code

🧩 How It Works

  • Readie proposes a set of learned startup snapshots rather than a single snapshot
  • Each snapshot is small, initializes quickly, and covers a fraction of agent-generated code; together the set covers most workloads
  • The snapshot set is learned from a large training workload by formulating snapshot construction as an optimization problem and solving it with an approximation algorithm
  • Training workload consists of 15K public and LLM-synthesized scripts

⚙️ Key Details

  • Startup latency reduced by 3–22× compared to existing approaches at the same storage budget
  • End-to-end runtime reduced by 1.3–3.3×
  • System categorized under Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

💡 Why It Matters

  • Learned snapshot sets achieve both compactness and broad coverage where single snapshots cannot
  • Faster sandbox startup improves responsiveness of AI agents that rely on iterative code execution
  • Gains are realized without increasing storage budget

#AIagents #codeexecution #sandboxes #latencyoptimization #machinelearningsystems

Source: WebAgents: Unbundling Agent Creation, Hosting, and Execution for an Agent-Native Web Source: SkillBuffBench: Measuring What Agent Skills Contribute across Harnesses, Models, Skill Access Modes and Memory Source: Readie: Low-Latency Code Sandboxes for AI Agents

item.title: SimCity Creator Will Wright Announces AI-Powered Memory Game MyMems
item.description:
SimCity Creator Will Wright Announces AI-Powered Memory Game MyMems

Will Wright, the creator of SimCity and The Sims, is developing a new mobile game called MyMems that uses artificial intelligence to turn personal memories into a social simulation. The title is designed to build a “toy world” from the player’s autobiography, allowing users to create private or shared worlds that reflect their personal experiences.

🧩 How It Works

MyMems functions as a “cozy world builder” with a deep social simulation underneath, according to Virginia McArthur, executive producer and GM at Gallium Studios. Players interact with the game by adding “memories,” such as speaking a short story to their phone, which are then generated into objects that can be placed on the game’s map.

The game includes AI-powered avatars that represent people in the player’s life. As the player adds more elements, the world evolves into what Wright describes as a “map of your psyche,” similar to the concept in the film Inside Out. The developers note that by having the player author content bit by bit, the experience avoids feeling like a cheat, encouraging a style reminiscent of Scribblenauts where AI generates specific elements like a high school.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Developer: Gallium Studios.
  • AI Technology: The game uses the “Behavior Engine” from Artificial Agency as a foundational technology.
  • Game Genre: Described as a “social simulation” with worlds built from personal memories.
  • Player Reception: Internal testing showed players, including Maitz’s daughter who dislikes AI, became “addicted” to a test app featuring a character creator.

💡 Why It Matters

The development of MyMems occurs in a landscape where AI integration in gaming is met with mixed reactions. Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick stated that generative AI has “zero part” in what Rockstar Games is building for GTA VI. Wright notes that his three sons are “pretty negative” on AI, though he views the technology as an “amazing tool.” Gallium Studios remains concerned about negative responses to generative AI but believes that letting players author the content mitigates resistance. MyMems will join other social simulations like Krafton’s Inzoi and Nintendo’s Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream.

🚀 Availability

MyMems is set to launch in 2027.

#MyMems #WillWright #GalliumStudios #SocialSimulation #GenerativeAI #MobileGaming

Source: Will Wright’s next game uses AI to map your memories

item.title: SMART SDK and AgentCore Simplify WhatsApp Agent Deployment on AWS
item.description:
SMART SDK and AgentCore Simplify WhatsApp Agent Deployment on AWS

Across Latin America, India, and Southeast Asia, WhatsApp is one of the most widely used messaging applications, but building a robust agent on top of it requires handling complex, type-dependent payloads, media processing pipelines, and strict compliance rules. To simplify this process, SMART (Social Messaging Agent Runtime Toolkit) is available as an open source Python SDK and Terraform stack that provides the full channel layer for agents running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

🧩 How it works

SMART allows you to provide an agent that runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, and it handles the underlying channel logic. The architecture utilizes the following services:

  • AWS End User Messaging Social: Receives inbound WhatsApp messages and routes them to the processing layer.
  • AWS Lambda: Handles the channel logic, including verifying SNS message signatures, normalizing payloads, and rate-limiting users (20 messages per minute by default).
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: Provides the runtime, memory, and observability for the agent.
  • Supporting Services: Amazon DynamoDB (optional, for per-user state), AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon CloudWatch, and Amazon S3 supply state management, credentials, monitoring, and storage.

The AgentCore runtime hosts and scales the agent without requiring infrastructure management. AgentCore memory persists conversation history across sessions and deployments, scoped automatically to each phone number. The create_session_manager() function binds the agent to this memory, with a default retention period of 7 days. Frameworks such as Strands Agents get memory wired automatically, while LangGraph and Pydantic-AI can integrate with the conversation loop.

⚙️ Key details

Wiring up a custom WhatsApp agent typically involves configuring more than 10 AWS services and learning specific system behaviors. SMART abstracts these complexities, including:

  • Inbound message authentication and normalization.
  • Processing pipelines for media such as voice notes, images, and documents.
  • Durable schedules for reminders and authenticated paths for external systems to trigger outbound messages.
  • Compliance with Meta’s requirement that messages sent more than 24 hours after the user’s last message must use pre-approved templates.
  • Handling of intermediate tool outputs (like button lists or progress updates) to prevent conversation history corruption.

🚀 Availability

SMART is an open source solution. A single command deploys the entire infrastructure to your AWS account. Webmotors, originally scoped as a two-month engagement, compressed delivery to six weeks and moved their internal team into controlled production ahead of a full launch using this approach.

#WhatsApp #AmazonBedrock #AIAgents #AWS #OpenSource

Source: Build WhatsApp AI agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Study: LLM Thinking Effort Boosts Confidence, Not Accuracy in Shopping Agents
item.description:
Study: LLM Thinking Effort Boosts Confidence, Not Accuracy in Shopping Agents

Researchers benchmarked ten frontier large language models (LLMs) acting as autonomous shopping agents to test whether increased computational effort improves purchase decisions. The study found that while “thinking harder” significantly raised the models’ stated confidence, it did not improve the actual quality of their product choices.

🔍 Overview

The study investigates two questions regarding LLMs deployed as shopping agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports accurately predict the likelihood of error? The work challenges the assumption that models with more thinking power inherently make higher-quality purchasing decisions.

🧩 How it works

The agents process multimodal product listings, utilizing both visual and text data, to recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. To evaluate this capability, the researchers benchmarked ten frontier models using three specific product-choice datasets:

  • WebShop: A general web shopping benchmark.
  • Amazon SQID: A platform dataset from Amazon.
  • Wayfair WANDS: A platform dataset from Wayfair.

⚙️ Key details

The results across all three benchmarks revealed several critical findings about model performance and reliability:

  • Confidence vs. Correctness: Increasing thinking effort raised stated confidence at a statistically significant level but did not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way.
  • Calibration: Most models were not well-calibrated at every effort level, meaning their reported confidence percentages did not match their true correctness percentages.
  • Shared Errors: Errors were strongly shared among models; when one model made an error in a task, several others tended to err on the same task.
  • Convergent Wrong Answers: On tasks where multiple models all made errors, a large number of them picked the same wrong product.

💡 Why it matters

This research highlights a divergence between the subjective assurance reported by LLMs and their objective decision-making accuracy in commercial contexts. It suggests that for autonomous shopping agents, additional computational resources may yield higher stated confidence without corresponding gains in correctness, which has implications for relying on these systems for financial or consumer decisions.

#LLM #AIagents #Calibration #Benchmarking #Shopping

Source: Thinking Harder Doesn’t Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents

item.title: Xing 4 LLM Series Advances Architecture and Training on Ascend Hardware
item.description:
Xing 4 LLM Series Advances Architecture and Training on Ascend Hardware

A new report details Xing 4, a series of large language models extending the TeleChat lineage through coordinated advances in model architecture and training infrastructure on Ascend hardware. The work spans architecture selection, large-scale pretraining, and reasoning and agentic post-training, culminating in a 285B-parameter model trained on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards.

🔍 Overview

  • Xing 4 extends the TeleChat lineage with coordinated architecture and infrastructure advances
  • Report covers architecture selection, large-scale pretraining, and reasoning and agentic post-training
  • Establishes an Ascend-oriented training foundation for continued development across model scales

🧩 How it works

  • Studies sparse activation, attention design, model depth and width, and speculative decoding to balance capacity with computation, memory access, and execution overhead
  • Pretraining infrastructure builds on MindSpore HyperParallel with:
    • Topology-aware hybrid sharding
    • Efficient distributed optimizer execution
    • Coordinated management of long-sequence workloads and activation memory
  • CPU affinity and core isolation reduce host scheduling interference
  • Post-training introduces TeleGym, a unified agent execution platform connecting execution, evaluation, and trajectory construction to policy optimization
  • TeleGym uses disaggregated asynchronous execution, bounded oversampling, and partial rollout to accommodate heterogeneous task durations while preserving trajectory continuity across policy updates

⚙️ Key details

  • 285B-parameter model pretrained on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards
  • Architecture studies cover sparse activation, attention design, model depth/width, speculative decoding
  • Infrastructure: MindSpore HyperParallel with topology-aware hybrid sharding, distributed optimizer execution, long-sequence and activation memory management
  • Post-training platform: TeleGym with disaggregated asynchronous execution, bounded oversampling, partial rollout
  • Foundation supports continued development across model scales and demanding reasoning and agent workloads

💡 Why it matters

  • Demonstrates end-to-end Ascend-oriented training pipeline from architecture to agentic post-training
  • Provides concrete system configuration (285B parameters, 8,192 Ascend 910C cards) for architectural and systems studies
  • TeleGym platform enables unified agent execution, evaluation, and policy optimization for reasoning workloads

#LLM #Ascend #TeleChat #MindSpore #AIAgents #DistributedTraining

Source: TeleChat to Xing4: Advancing Frontier Agentic Models on Domestic Chips and Frameworks

item.title: XMimic Trains Humanoid Motion Tracking 3.7x Faster Than BlinkMimic
item.description:
XMimic Trains Humanoid Motion Tracking 3.7x Faster Than BlinkMimic

🚀 Overview

XMimic is a new AI development that trains whole-body motion tracking for the Unitree G1 robot 3.7 times faster than the previous BlinkMimic method when using four H100 GPUs. The improvement comes from rebuilding BlinkMimic’s world-model trainer in JAX, enabling faster training while maintaining the same quality.

🧩 How it works

XMimic implements the same algorithm as BlinkMimic but runs entirely in JAX. This includes the simulator (MuJoCo Warp through MJX), the replay buffer, the world model, the policy and the critic. The entire training iterations compile into single XLA programs, so the GPU never waits for Python. The system can distribute iterations across 2 to 4 GPUs working simultaneously.

⚙️ Key details

  • Speed: Reaches BlinkMimic’s target in 0.86 minutes on four H100s (vs. 3.19 minutes on one); on a single H100, XMimic is 1.3 times faster
  • Quality: Both methods achieve the same normalized evaluation return (0.86–0.87) with no clip failures after 6 minutes of training
  • Target: Normalized evaluation return ≥ 0.82 with none of the 40 LAFAN1 clips failing, held for three consecutive checkpoints
  • GPU usage: Uses slightly more total GPU time (3.4 vs. 3.2 GPU-minutes) but the speedup buys wall-clock time
  • Hardware: One H100 NVL per GPU, GPUs connected by NVLink in a node
  • Training: All methods ran on the same cluster; every 100th checkpoint is evaluated on all 40 clips with 4 replicas each
  • Hyperparameters: Uses BlinkMimic’s hyperparameters (PRESET[main], commit d264658)

The development is detailed in the paper XMimic and XSoma: Learning Humanoid Motion Tracking and Locomotion in Under a Minute by Nico Bohlinger and Jan Peters (2026).

📄 Availability

XMimic replaces the first version which covered XMimic alone. It is accompanied by XSoma, which applies the same recipe for locomotion on rough terrain. Please cite the paper if you use XMimic:

XMimic and XSoma: Learning Humanoid Motion Tracking and Locomotion in Under a Minute (Nico Bohlinger, Jan Peters, 2026)

#AI #Robotics #JAX #MotionTracking #Humanoid

Source: nico-bohlinger/xmimic

item.title: .NET SDK enables development of applications using the A2A v1.0 protocol
item.description:
.NET SDK enables development of applications using the A2A v1.0 protocol

A new .NET SDK has been released that allows developers to build and host applications following the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, providing a robust implementation of the specification v1.0.

🧩 How it works

The library supports multiple communication methods, allowing agents to interact through message-based or task-based patterns.

  • Agent Capability Discovery: Retrieves agent capabilities and metadata through agent cards.
  • Message-based Communication: Enables direct, stateless messaging with immediate responses.
  • Task-based Communication: Allows for the creation and management of persistent, long-running agent tasks.
  • Streaming Support: Facilitates real-time communication using Server-Sent Events.

⚙️ Key details

The SDK is built to integrate directly with web application stacks and supports multiple protocol bindings.

Component Description
A2AClient Primary client for making A2A requests to agents; supports streaming, non-streaming, and push notifications.
A2ACardResolver Resolves agent card information from A2A-compatible endpoints.
A2AServer Core server handling A2A JSON-RPC requests and coordinating task lifecycle.
IAgentHandler Interface for agents to implement, providing methods for message handling and task cancellation.
TaskUpdater API for emitting task lifecycle events such as start, complete, and fail.
MessageResponder API for sending stateless message replies without task lifecycle management.

All three protocol bindings—JSON-RPC, HTTP+JSON REST, and gRPC—share the same client contract and server pipeline. The gRPC binding is packaged as optional modules to prevent core consumers from being forced to depend on specific gRPC libraries.

🚀 Availability

The library targets .NET 8 and higher and includes built-in extensions for hosting A2A agents within web applications.

  • The v1.0 implementation is available as a NuGet package.
  • A backward-compatible package is available during the transition period.
  • A configuration option allows developers to explicitly request a completed task response when calling v1 servers from v0.3 clients, which helps avoid returning an incomplete initial task snapshot.

#dotnet #AIagents #A2A #softwaredevelopment #protocol

Source: a2aproject/a2a-dotnet

item.title: A2A Protocol SDK Overview

item.title: AgnostUI Local v2 copies UI components into your project for AI readability
item.description:
AgnostUI Local v2 copies UI components into your project for AI readability

AgnostUI Local (v2) is a new CLI-based UI component library that copies components directly into your project at install time. Instead of keeping components hidden inside node_modules, the source code lands directly in your repository, providing full control and native integration with your framework.

🧩 How it works

AgnostUI components are authored as Lit Web Components, a standards-based layer over native Custom Elements. The CLI wraps these components for your specific framework at copy time. By default, components are placed under src/components/ag/, creating a dedicated namespace that keeps AgnosticUI components separate from your own code. This approach ensures that your design system does not fork when your tech stack changes.

🤖 AI and Agent Integration

Because the component source lives locally, it is readable by AI tools such as Cursor, Claude, Copilot, Windsurf, Aider, Gemini, Replit, Kiro, and Antigravity. Every tool sees the raw source, creating a high-fidelity environment for Generative UI and agent-driven interfaces.

  • Reduce Hallucination: Since the LLM reads local files like any other code, it knows exactly what is possible, preventing invented props or APIs.
  • Better Token Efficiency: Using semantic HTML and standard CSS provides clean context, allowing agents to spend fewer tokens to understand the UI for faster, more accurate generations.
  • Agent Skills: AgnosticUI Playbooks act as pre-defined skills, prompting agents to scaffold complex, accessible workflows using local components.

📜 Playbooks and Components

The schema-driven layer ships with three companion documents. AgnosticUI offers Playbooks that demonstrate modular, prompt-driven UI components. These Playbooks support agent-generated UI workflows directly.

💡 Why it matters

AgnostUI Local solves the “Black Box” problem of traditional libraries hidden in node_modules. It is designed as the architecture for the next era of development, characterized as context-aware, framework-agnostic, and AI-ready.

item.title: Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base and AgentCore Memory Integration
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base and AgentCore Memory Integration

Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory have been updated to include integrated conversation storage, fact extraction, and intelligent retrieval. This capability allows developers to streamline the process of maintaining context across sessions by automating fact-based retrieval and knowledge base interactions.

🧩 How it works

By adding a memoryConfiguration to the AgenticRetrieveStream request, AgentCore memory functions as a retrieval source alongside a knowledge base. The integration follows these operational steps:

  • Conversation Management: The service stores each conversation and extracts facts from it.
  • Planning: The planner autonomously decides when a stored fact about the user is relevant.
  • Query Composition: Retrieved facts are used to compose sub-queries sent to the knowledge base.
  • Persistence: After an answer is generated, the service saves the turn back to memory.

⚙️ Key details

The integration enables robust access control and user-specific memory, as illustrated by the following table of operational roles:

Component Role
Amazon Cognito Authenticates employees and provides sub and email claims
AgentCore Memory Stores facts, conversation history, and user context
Managed Knowledge Base Performs ACL-enabled retrieval based on user context
Planner Determines when to use long-term memory to aid sub-queries

💡 Implementation Requirements

  • Opt-in Compatibility: The feature is opt-in and backward compatible.
  • Security: The application remains responsible for authenticating the user and passing identity information. The userContext ensures the knowledge base returns only documents permitted by the user’s access control lists (ACLs).
  • IAM Roles: The handler assumes the application’s IAM role using the user ID as a session tag.

#AmazonBedrock #GenerativeAI #AIAgents #CloudComputing

Source: Build memory-aware AI agents with Agentic Retrieve on Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Ax Ships a TypeScript-First, Multi-Language LLM Toolkit
item.description:
Ax Ships a TypeScript-First, Multi-Language LLM Toolkit

Ax is a TypeScript-first development toolkit that ships as @ax-llm/ax. Its shared semantic core is also compiled into generated Python, Java, C++, Go, and Rust libraries.

🔍 Overview

Ax provides typed structured generation, deployment profiles, agents, flows, and optimizers. The TypeScript package is the source implementation and current published package.

🧩 How it works

Signatures for typed structured generation can be written using:

  • A string DSL
  • The fluent f() builder
  • Any Standard Schema v1 validator, including Zod, Valibot, and ArkType

The deployment name selects wire behavior, while the model ID is resolved inside that deployment. Named deployment profiles cover native APIs, routers, hosted inference, configurable runtimes, audio, and realtime event streams.

For example:

1
2
3

const llm = ai({ name: "openai", apiKey: process.env.OPENAI_APIKEY });
const classify = ax('review:string -> sentiment:class "positive, negative, neutral"',);
await classify.forward(llm, { review: "This product is amazing!" })

The evidence describes this example as requiring no prompt engineering. The provider name can be switched from "openai" to "anthropic", "google-gemini", "meta", "together", "fireworks", "deepseek", or "grok", among others.

⚙️ Key details

  • Agents: runtime execution, context budgets, checkpoints, action-log replay, discovery, memory, skills, and delegation.
  • Flows: typed program graphs supporting branches, loops, feedback, cache behavior, parallel execution, and .returns(...) projection.
  • Optimizers: GEPA, few-shot bootstrapping, portable optimizer artifacts, and evaluation/apply flows.
  • Runtime path: Ax is designed to stay in the same latency class as direct provider calls while adding typed outputs, validation, retries, tools, tracing, and memory. Its hot path renders the signature, calls the provider, parses the result, and returns a typed value.
  • Streaming: Streaming is the default. Ax can parse fields as they arrive, run streaming assertions, fail early, cancel an in-flight stream, and start correction.

🚀 Availability

Language Package or distribution Availability
TypeScript / JavaScript @ax-llm/ax Published on npm
Python axllm Published on PyPI
Java dev.axllm:ax Published on Maven Central
C++ axllm::axllm CMake FetchContent source build
Go github.com/ax-llm/ax/packages/go Installable with go get
Rust axllm Published on crates.io

The same signatures, provider mappings, agents, flows, runtime contracts, and optimizers are compiled into verified generated Python, Java, C++, Go, and Rust libraries.

#AI #LLMDevelopment #TypeScript #AIAgents #OpenSource

Source: ax-llm/ax

item.title: BigQuery Agent Analytics SDK for AI Agent Observability
item.description:
BigQuery Agent Analytics SDK for AI Agent Observability

An open-source Python SDK for analyzing, evaluating, and curating agent traces stored in BigQuery has been released. Built on top of the BigQuery Agent Analytics, it provides a consumption-layer toolkit for agent observability, analysis, evaluation, and advanced capabilities like the Agent Context Graph — extracting decision traces from your agent’s context graph — at scale.

🔍 Overview

  • An open-source Python SDK for analyzing, evaluating, and curating agent traces stored in BigQuery.
  • Built on top of the BigQuery Agent Analytics, it provides a consumption-layer toolkit for agent observability, analysis, evaluation, and advanced capabilities like the Agent Context Graph — extracting decision traces from your agent’s context graph — at scale.

⚙️ Key details

  • The BigQuery Agent Analytics SDK connects your AI agent telemetry in BigQuery to a rich set of evaluation, observability, and analytics capabilities.
  • It is designed for ML engineers, data scientists, and platform teams who run agents in production and need to understand agent behavior, measure quality, and detect regressions — all through BigQuery SQL or Python.
  • Features include:
    • Trace reconstruction and DAG visualization
    • Per-event-type BigQuery views
    • Observability dashboards (Looker Studio, Streamlit, SQL, and BigFrames), including BQCA Prompt & Response Logging dashboards for Conversational Analytics data agents
    • System metrics (latency, turn count, tool call error rate, token efficiency, time to first token, cost)
    • Performance Metrics (correctness, hallucination, sentiment, efficiency, etc)
    • Multi-trial system and performance metrics
    • Grader composition (weighted, binary, majority strategies)
    • Eval suite lifecycle management with graduation and saturation detection
    • Static quality validation (ambiguous tasks, class imbalance, suspicious thresholds)
    • BigQuery AI.GENERATE, AI.EMBED, AI.CLASSIFY
    • Anomaly detection and latency forecasting
    • Categorical (Hatteras-style) evaluation via BigFrames
    • Agent Context Graph — extract decision traces from your agent’s context graph: the requests an agent handled, the options it weighed, and the outcomes it committed, materialized into a queryable BigQuery property graph (GQL traversal, scheduled refresh via bqaa context-graph)
    • Long-horizon cross-session memory
    • Multi-stage agent insights pipeline
    • Drift detection for golden vs production question distributions
    • 12+ commands for diagnostics, evaluation, and CI/CD integration
    • Remote Function (BigQuery SQL via Cloud Run)
    • Python UDF scoring kernels
    • Streaming evaluation (Cloud Scheduler + Cloud Run)
    • Continuous query templates

🚀 Availability

  • Python 3.10+
  • A Google Cloud project with BigQuery enabled
  • Agent traces already written to BigQuery by one of the producers above

💡 Why it matters

  • Provides a comprehensive toolkit for AI agent observability, analysis, evaluation, and advanced capabilities at scale.
  • Designed for ML engineers, data scientists, and platform teams to understand agent behavior, measure quality, and detect regressions.
  • Enables trace reconstruction, DAG visualization, and observability dashboards for better agent performance insights.
  • Facilitates system metrics, performance metrics, and eval suite lifecycle management for continuous improvement.
  • Supports anomaly detection, latency forecasting, and categorical evaluation for robust agent performance.
  • Provides the Agent Context Graph for extracting decision traces and long-horizon cross-session memory for enhanced agent capabilities.
  • Offers multi-stage agent insights pipeline and drift detection for golden vs production question distributions.
  • Includes 12+ commands for diagnostics, evaluation, and CI/CD integration for seamless workflow integration.
  • Supports Remote Function, Python UDF scoring kernels, and streaming evaluation for flexible evaluation capabilities.
  • Provides continuous query templates for efficient query management.
