item.title: SAP and Infosys Argue Enterprise AI Needs Unified Data and Governance
item.description:
SAP and Infosys Argue Enterprise AI Needs Unified Data and Governance

SAP and Infosys executives are advocating for a shift in how enterprises approach AI, moving away from isolated pilots toward a unified platform model that integrates data, governance, and business processes.

🧩 From Pilots to Enterprise Platform

For years, organizations have treated AI as a series of discrete experiments. However, as AI agents begin to move into workflows that run the business, that model is becoming inadequate. The core challenge now is rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together to turn AI into part of the enterprise operating model.

Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, notes that many customers struggle to convert interest in AI into an operationalized model because programs often start as isolated proof-of-concepts (POCs) on inconsistent and fragmented data foundations. This fragmentation leads to duplication, inconsistent performance, and no clear path to scale.

⚙️ Key Components of the Shift

  • Unified Data Layer: Leiduck argues that AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation. Companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes.
  • Governance and Oversight: Clear policies, access controls, monitoring, and oversight are necessary to ensure agents remain trustworthy and aligned with business requirements. Leiduck and Singh agree that the absence of governance does not speed up adoption but instead creates a “risk backlog” that can force disruptive stops and audits.
  • Evaluation Framework: Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, recommends evaluating AI use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability. Companies must identify where an agent can move meaningful business metrics, ensure their data and talent can support the use case, and establish whether successful applications can be replicated.

💡 Why It Matters

As AI moves into mission-critical workflows, the stakes change significantly. Leiduck points out that while “80% might be good enough” for everyday applications, that level of accuracy is a “very terrible result” in areas such as supply chains or financial close. The goal is to move beyond AI as a mere productivity tool to “AI as a decision-making partner” that helps leaders understand what is happening, anticipate what comes next, and determine how to respond. Customer-specific knowledge graphs and governed data are becoming critical enterprise assets in this future.

#EnterpriseAI #AIAgents #SAP #Infosys #DataGovernance

Source: Building AI that can work across the enterprise

item.title: Synadia Agent Protocol Connects AI Agents Through NATS
item.description:
Synadia Agent Protocol Connects AI Agents Through NATS

The Synadia Agent Protocol for NATS lets AI agents register as agents micro services that callers can discover, prompt, and stream from using the same wire format. The project includes TypeScript and Python caller and host SDKs, along with pre-built plugins for connecting existing AI harnesses to NATS.

🔍 How it works

  • Each agent registers as an agents micro service and serves the protocol’s prompt, status, and hb endpoints.
  • Subjects follow the pattern agents.{verb}.{token}.{owner}.{session}, where verb is prompt, hb, or status.
  • The protocol can be used with Codex, OpenCode, Claude Code, OpenClaw, PI, Hermes, Flue, or a custom agent.

🧩 SDKs and plugins

The SDKs are split into caller and host packages in both TypeScript and Python:

Component Role
Caller SDK (client-sdk/) Discovers and prompts agents.
Host SDK (agent-sdk/) Registers and serves an agent.

Caller-only consumers install the caller package; authors hosting agents install both halves of their language’s pair. A cross-SDK interoperability test runs the TypeScript reference agent against the Python client to validate the shared wire format.

Pre-built channel plugins connect existing AI harnesses to NATS without writing code. The active SDK release rollout roadmap tracks sender identity, extension hooks, compatibility, integration adoption, dependency controls, and release promotion.

⚙️ Extensions and applications

Tracing is not part of this release. The SDKs provide generic extension hooks, including prompt and request interceptors, extra envelope fields, and heartbeat extras; tracing extensions can be built in separate packages.

Apps built on the SDKs include:

  • A Vue 3 browser client for discovery, prompting with attachments, streaming, and inline mid-stream query allow or deny.
  • A control plane that spawns sessions when it discovers a headless controller and fans a single prompt across multiple working directories in parallel.
  • A process that spawns and manages headless Claude Code sessions, each registering as a first-class agent at agents.prompt.cc-headless.<owner>.<session>.

#NATS #AIAgents #AgentProtocol #TypeScript #Python

Source: synadia-ai/synadia-agents

item.title: TruLens and BitRouter Enhance AI Agent Cost & Quality with OpenTelemetry
item.description:
TruLens and BitRouter Enhance AI Agent Cost & Quality with OpenTelemetry

TruLens and BitRouter, two open‑source tools, recently released updates that improve the reliability and cost‑efficiency of AI agents by leveraging OpenTelemetry observability and intelligent routing.

🔍 Overview

  • TruLens instrumentation built on OpenTelemetry.
  • BitRouter runs locally and exposes an OpenAI‑compatible API.

🧩 How it Works

  • TruLens instruments every function call, LLM generation, retrieval, and tool invocation as structured OTEL span.
  • Tracing is portable to any OTLP backend; export to Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, Datadog, New Relic, or any OTLP‑compatible backend.
  • BitRouter uses a Rust router between agents and model providers; routing policy lives in files you own; routes are inspectable and diffable; policy changes only when published; it learns from outcomes and proposes new policies.

⚙️ Key Details

  • TruLens records latency, inputs, outputs, tokens, cost per step; provides scores, latency, cost per app version; cheapest version often not worst.
  • TruLens judges graded against human annotations; 95% Agent errors caught with Agent GPA on TRAIL/GAIA; 267/281 human‑annotated errors vs 55% baseline trace judge.
  • Performance metrics: 0.81 Groundedness F1 on LLM‑AggreFact, 0.93 Context relevance NDCG@5, first of five tools on three of four ranking metrics, 4.2:1 context relevance adversarial win‑loss.
  • BitRouter cut API cost by 40.9% on Terminal‑Bench 2.1 while maintaining nearly same reward; dynamic routing between GPT‑5.6, Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4 Flash; savings due to routing decisions, not cheaper models.
  • Companies using TruLens: Walmart Global Tech, Cisco, J.P. Morgan Chase, Equinix, VMware by Broadcom, Hitachi Digital Services, Thomson Reuters, phData, HID Global.
  • BitRouter supports OpenAI Chat Completions, Anthropic Messages, cross‑protocol routing; includes built‑in Codex and Claude support.

🚀 Availability

  • TruLens is open source and OpenTelemetry‑native.
  • BitRouter runs locally, provides an OpenAI‑compatible API; requires minimal changes; can be installed with npx skills add bitrouter/bitrouter; hosted routing presets use @<name>; local bitrouter/auto selector requires a local router.
  • Official macOS distributions support Apple Silicon (arm64) only; run bro for line‑based first‑run setup; native harness interfaces via bro claude, bro codex, bro launch <agent>.

💡 Why it Matters

  • TruLens enables tracing of every agent step, making errors traceable and providing clear cost‑quality trade‑offs.
  • BitRouter reduces API cost while maintaining performance by intelligent routing, demonstrating the value of routing decisions.

#OpenTelemetry #AIagents #CostOptimization #Observability #OpenSource

Source: truera/trulens Source: bitrouter/bitrouter

item.title: TurboVLA: Real-Time Vision-Language-Action Model
item.description:
TurboVLA: Real-Time Vision-Language-Action Model

🔍 Overview

TurboVLA is a real-time vision-language-action model that achieves 32 Hz on an RTX 4090 with <1 GB VRAM.

🧩 How it works

TurboVLA adopts a direct V+L→A mapping instead of using a large language model as the central interface. It independently encodes visual observations and language instructions, directly exchanging information between them through lightweight bidirectional vision-language interaction.

⚙️ Key details

  • Achieves an 88.06% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0.
  • Achieves 97.6% average success with only 0.2B parameters, 31.2ms inference latency, and 0.9GiB inference VRAM on a consumer-grade RTX 4090.
  • A 0.4B TurboVLA achieves 88.06% success on RoboTwin 2.0, even matching or outperforming substantially larger VLA policies.

🚀 Availability

  • Clone the repository: git clone https://github.com/H-EmbodVis/TurboVLA.git
  • Use Python 3.9.25 for the LIBERO reference environment and Python 3.10 for RoboTwin.
  • Install torch==2.3.1 torchvision==0.18.1 –index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu121 for the LIBERO environment.
  • Released the TurboVLA model checkpoints on Hugging Face.
  • Released the paper, training and evaluation code.
  • Released the LIBERO inference latency benchmark code.

💡 Why it matters

TurboVLA achieves high performance without requiring an LLM-centric execution pathway. It directly constructs task-conditioned representations while avoiding the overhead of an LLM-centric execution pathway.

#AIagents #ComputerVision #MachineLearning

Source: H-EmbodVis/TurboVLA

item.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime V2 Improves Session Startup and Billing
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime V2 Improves Session Startup and Billing

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime provides a fully managed, serverless environment where each session runs in its own isolated microVM, scales to zero when idle, and you only pay for the resources your sessions consume.

🔍 Overview

  • AgentCore runtime runs each session in a new microVM.
  • The platform scales to zero when there’s no work and charges only for consumed resources.

🧩 How V2 Starts a Session

  • Setting platformVersion to “V2” changes how sessions start.
  • When you create or update a runtime, AgentCore starts your container in a fresh microVM and waits for the first healthy ping (GET /ping) within 120 seconds.
  • It then clears the operating system’s file cache, freezes the microVM, and stores its memory and disk as a snapshot. Building this snapshot takes a few minutes during create or update.

⚙️ Session Execution

  • On a new session, AgentCore restores the snapshot into a new microVM.
  • Your process resumes exactly where it was frozen, with imports, objects, and clients in place.
  • Files from the image are loaded lazily; each block is fetched the first time a session reads it and then cached closer to the host.
  • Anything held at snapshot time, including RAM‑backed file systems such as /dev/shm, is available at memory speed from the first access.
  • The file cache is cleared before the freeze, so reads during init do not speed up restored sessions.
  • A CLI that runs as a separate process and exits, or a browser binary, is read during init and then fetched again from the image for each restored session.

🚀 Performance Benefits

  • Session start times are faster and more consistent.
  • V2 reclaims memory that sessions don’t use, so billing tracks what the agent actually uses.
  • For most agents, switching to V2 is all it takes.

📏 Measuring Startup Time

  • AgentCore publishes CloudWatch metrics in the AWS/Bedrock-AgentCore namespace.
  • Latency: time to first byte.
  • OverheadLatency: platform overhead such as microVM start and snapshot restore on a new session.

🛠️ Tips for Agents

  • With the AgentCore Python SDK, init means everything before app.run().
  • If you run your own HTTP server (Node.js or another language), report healthy only after your initialization finishes.
  • Build hooks are now supported to keep work off the first request.

#AmazonBedrock #AgentCore #Serverless

Source: Architecture patterns for fast session startup on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime | Amazon Web Services

item.title: OpenAI Launches ChatGPT Wallet for Dots AI Agents to Make Purchases
item.description:
OpenAI Launches ChatGPT Wallet for Dots AI Agents to Make Purchases

OpenAI is launching ChatGPT Wallet, allowing its Dots AI agents platform to make purchases on behalf of users in response to prompts.

🧩 How it works

  • Prompt-based buying: Once a card is added to the wallet, Dots agents can buy items in response to user prompts.
  • User checkout review: Agents check in with the user each time before completing checkout.
  • Biometric verification: OpenAI’s support page states every purchase requires a security check using biometric verification like Face ID or a fingerprint scan.
  • Payment tokenization: OpenAI substitutes actual credit card details with a payment token—similar to tap to pay, Apple Pay, or Google Wallet—so card information is never shared with the Dots agent or the seller.

🚀 Availability

ChatGPT Wallet is rolling out starting today, subject to specific account and card requirements:

  • Eligible users: ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US who are aged 18 and older and have a US billing address.
  • Supported cards: Eligible US-issued American Express, Chase, Mastercard, and Visa cards.

⚙️ Limitations and future features

  • Retailer blockades: ChatGPT Wallet might not work everywhere because some retailers block or restrict AI agents. Earlier this year, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agents.
  • System requirements: OpenAI stated that websites need to ensure agents are not inadvertently blocked and that risk systems recognize legitimate agent transactions.
  • Planned automation: OpenAI expects to eventually allow users to delegate purchases entirely by pre-approving transactions within set parameters, such as spending limits, time periods, or purchase categories.

#OpenAI #ChatGPTWallet #AIAgents #DotsAI #Fintech

Source: ChatGPT Wallet lets OpenAI’s Dots agents make purchases for you

item.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Updates Deliver Faster, More Efficient AI Agents
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Updates Deliver Faster, More Efficient AI Agents

Amazon has announced updates to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a managed compute layer designed to help developers build, connect, and optimize AI agents securely at scale. The new version addresses the growing complexity of running AI agents in production by improving speed, efficiency, and resource management.

📈 Agent Adoption and Capabilities

The length of tasks that frontier agents can complete on their own doubles about every four months. Enterprise adoption is rising, with 40 percent of large enterprises scaling AI agents, up from 27 percent a year ago. These agents do more than traditional software; they execute code, navigate browsers, access sensitive data, and act on behalf of users.

⚠️ Infrastructure Challenges

As organizations move from deploying a handful of agents to running thousands of concurrent sessions, building and managing custom sandboxes becomes increasingly complex and expensive. Pre-provisioned environments consume resources even when idle, driving up costs, while on-demand environments introduce cold-start latency. Only 15 percent of organizations have scaled orchestrated, multi-agent systems, and 70 percent say they cannot yet trust and govern their agents.

🛠️ Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore helps developers build, connect, and optimize agents securely at scale. The AgentCore runtime is a managed compute layer that provides a fully managed environment to deploy and run agents without building or maintaining infrastructure. The core guarantee remains that every session runs in its own hardware-isolated Firecracker micro virtual machine (MicroVM), with its own identity, policy, and audit trail.

🚀 Key Runtime Updates

The next generation AgentCore runtime meets demands for scale and speed. The updates include:

Feature Improvement Details
Startup Speed 15x faster Sessions start in under 2 seconds, independent of image size and concurrency
Compute Scaling 4x more Supports up to 8 vCPUs and 32 GB, with container images up to 10 GB
Efficiency 68% more efficient Improved resource utilization while maintaining isolation boundaries
Memory Footprint Reduced by ~60% Lower memory usage per invocation in many use cases
Infrastructure No warm pools needed Eliminates the need for pre-provisioned clusters to manage cold starts

💼 Enterprise Use Cases

Several organizations are leveraging the updated runtime to power their agents:

  • Mission: Uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime to power a natural-language query agent that helps users retrieve property and sales insights.
  • Zuora: Uses the runtime to run automation and AI agents on its cloud, relying on efficient and reliable infrastructure.
  • Rescale: Uses the runtime to deploy engineering-specific agents that validate simulation inputs, troubleshoot jobs, and generate reports.

The new AgentCore runtime gives these organizations a compelling combination of faster agent experiences and more efficient resource utilization as they bring enterprise agents into production.

#AIAgents #AmazonBedrock #CloudInfrastructure #EnterpriseAI #MachineLearning

Source: Run agents securely and efficiently with the next generation AgentCore runtime | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Anthropic releases Claude Duet, a consumer‑friendly AI work assistant
item.description:
Anthropic releases Claude Duet, a consumer‑friendly AI work assistant

Claude Duet is Anthropic’s newest AI agent aimed at consumers who want help with work without writing code. The author tested it for a week while juggling a busy travel and work schedule.

🔍 Overview

  • Claude Duet is positioned as a consumer‑friendly, work‑focused AI agent.
  • It follows earlier Anthropic agents: Claude Code (a coding agent) → Claude Cowork (more consumer‑friendly) → Claude Duet (most consumer‑friendly and work‑oriented).
  • Other recent agents mentioned in the landscape are Instinct’s text‑based assistant, Meta’s Muse, and OpenAI’s Dots.

⚙️ How it works

  • Users connect productivity and chat services (email, calendar, Google Docs, Slack). Duet then scans the data and surfaces suggestions as swipeable cards, similar to a “to‑do list Tinder.”
  • Each morning Duet greets the user, highlights key items (e.g., packing for a video shoot), and proposes to‑dos with offers to draft messages or add agenda items.
  • By accessing a biweekly staff‑meeting summary email and Slack, Duet linked a meeting comment to a direct Slack message.
  • Access to a shared Google Doc let Duet identify the user’s manager for weekly 1:1 meetings.

📋 Key Details

  • Design – Cheery, minimalist Claude design; app described as consumer‑friendly and approachable.
  • Platform – Available as a standalone app, now fully supports the iPhone Duo.
  • Interaction style – Swipe left/right on suggestion cards; drafted messages are tagged “sent with Claude.”
  • Personalization – Mirrors the user’s writing habits (e.g., all‑lowercase style) and occasionally adds playful asides.
  • Data usage – Operates on data the user opts‑in to share; Anthropic notes ongoing testing of its judgment about when to message.

🚀 Availability

  • Claude Duet is a “research preview.”
  • Access limited to Pro, Max, and Ultra subscribers in the United States, with a waitlist for additional users.
  • Intended for “professionals and small business owners,” not for casual tasks like ordering food.

💡 Why it matters

  • Compared to Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots, Duet is described as “even more focused on work.”
  • It pushes the idea that AI agents can be useful for non‑programmers by handling everyday professional workflows.
  • The swipe‑card interface and daily brief aim to make AI assistance feel like a natural extension of existing productivity tools.

📊 Comparison to other agents

Agent Primary focus
Claude Duet Consumer‑friendly work assistance
Claude Cowork More consumer‑friendly than Claude Code
Claude Code Coding assistance

item.title: CLI tool adds automated scoring and checklist for Agent projects
item.description:
CLI tool adds automated scoring and checklist for Agent projects

The agent-handbook project released a new CLI tool that can automatically score an Agent codebase against a five‑pillar checklist drawn from its 31‑chapter Chinese handbook.

🔍 Overview

  • Provides a static scan of your Agent project and reports which of the five pillars are missing.
  • Maps gaps to the exact chapter and section of the handbook that explains the concept.
  • Generates a 0–10 score with concrete remediation suggestions.

🛠️ How it works

  • The command handbook doctor . walks the code, checks it against the five‑pillar criteria, and produces a Markdown table of results.
  • --md flag outputs the table so it can be pasted directly into an issue, README, or PR comment; the tool also posts the report automatically to the PR and the Job Summary.
  • handbook search <keyword> performs full‑text search across all 31 chapters, returning chapter, line number, and snippet.
  • handbook new <name> scaffolds a new Agent project that already satisfies all five pillars, earning a full score.
  • The tool runs with zero dependencies, using only the Python standard library, and works offline because the handbook data is bundled with the package.

⚙️ Key details

Command Description
handbook doctor . Five‑pillar health check, 0–10 score + remediation suggestions
handbook doctor . --md Output Markdown table for easy inclusion in issues/README
handbook search 上下文压缩 Full‑text search of the 31‑chapter handbook, returns chapter, line, snippet
handbook new my-agent Generate an Agent skeleton that scores full on the five pillars
Chapter Title Quick note
00 新手快速入门 10 分钟跑通第一个 Agent
03 LangGraph 图编排 复杂工作流、状态机、检查点
04 CrewAI 多智能体 角色化团队、任务分配

11 MCP 协议 标准化工具连接（含 2026 无状态核心）

16 调试与可观测性 LangSmith、日志、追踪

99 中英对照术语表 130+ 术语通俗解释

🚀 Availability

  • Alternative: pipx run agent-handbook doctor .

item.title: Natera Improves Lab Operations with Agentic AI System SWARM
item.description:
Natera Improves Lab Operations with Agentic AI System SWARM

Natera has deployed SWARM (Systematic Workflow Analytics and Resolutions Manager), an agentic AI system built with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to optimize lab instrument maintenance and reduce downtime. By digitizing institutional knowledge, the system assists service engineers in diagnosing equipment issues more efficiently.

🔍 Overview

Natera’s lab operations previously faced challenges with instrument downtime, leading to delays in sample processing and patient reporting. With an average first response time of 17.4 hours and over 65 tickets daily, the team sought a solution to leverage deep institutional knowledge rather than relying on fragmented, individual expertise.

🧩 How it works

SWARM utilizes a two-runtime architecture that shares a single library of skills to address maintenance tickets:

Component Function
swarm-agent Autonomously generates structured diagnostic reports before an engineer opens a ticket
swarm-hive Allows engineers to interact in real time, upload images, and explore troubleshooting paths

The system operates across four primary layers:

  • Event layer: Routes Jira tickets using Amazon EventBridge and Amazon SQS.
  • Agent layer: Hosts the swarm-agent, swarm-hive, and the skill library.
  • Context layer: Accesses vendor manuals, historical tickets, and operational data.
  • Observability and delivery layer: Captures logs, traces, and metrics.

⚙️ Key details

Natera opted for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to handle infrastructure orchestration, security, and scaling. Key security measures include:

  • Keyless deployment: Uses OIDC and AWS STS to generate short-lived, scoped credentials rather than long-lived keys.
  • Least privilege: AWS IAM enforces access control at the component level.
  • Network isolation: Amazon VPC with private subnets and endpoints restricts traffic.
  • Credential management: AWS Secrets Manager automatically rotates existing credentials every 30 days.

💡 Why it matters

Since implementing the system, Natera reports a 130x faster first response time and 96.2 percent automated coverage across support tickets. Ariel Jirau, who led the lab engineering team, noted, “The system does not replace engineers—it gives them access to the full depth of institutional knowledge the moment a ticket arrives.”

#AWS #AmazonBedrock #AgenticAI #Natera #LabOps

Source: How Natera designed an agentic AI system for lab ops with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Trustabl Introduces Open-Source Agent Reliability Analyzer for AI Agent Code
item.description:
Trustabl Introduces Open-Source Agent Reliability Analyzer for AI Agent Code

Trustabl’s Agent Reliability Analyzer is an open-source, deterministic scanner designed to find and fix reliability failures in AI agent code before it reaches production.

🔍 Overview

The Agent Reliability Analyzer performs deterministic static analysis across agent code to locate and resolve potential production failures. It operates entirely on your local machine without requiring a cloud scanner, an account, code uploads, or an LLM.

🧩 How it works

The tool scans an agent repository for gaps that break agents in production and applies fixes directly to the source code with a single command.

It detects specific vulnerabilities and failure points, including:

  • Tool descriptions that are too vague for a model to determine when to use them
  • Missing retry and timeout handling
  • Untyped parameters
  • Absent guardrails
  • Tool grants that exceed what the agent claims to do

⚙️ Key details

As of October 2026, the analyzer includes the following coverage metrics and architecture specs:

Feature Details
Rules 340+ rules
SDKs 9 SDKs
Languages 7 languages
Scopes 5 scopes
Engine Structure One agent reliability engine, ten front doors

🚀 Execution and installation

Scanning runs locally using standard commands:

  • Run directly via Docker: docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/repo" ghcr.io/trustabl/trustabl:latest scan /repo
  • Install via Homebrew: brew install trustabl/tap/trustabl

💡 Why it matters

While traditional scanners generate report files, Trustabl applies patches directly to the source code. This approach follows the design principle that reliability is engineered before deployment rather than observed after deployment.

#Trustabl #AIAgents #StaticAnalysis #OpenSource #SoftwareTesting

Source: trustabl/agent-reliability-analyzer

item.title: Agent Development Lifecycle Improves Reliability of Enterprise LLM Agents
item.description:
Agent Development Lifecycle Improves Reliability of Enterprise LLM Agents

Enterprise teams are shipping large language model (LLM) systems that call tools, orchestrate APIs, and answer questions over internal knowledge. A new Agent Development Lifecycle (Agent DLC) introduces a single explicit standard for judging every change and provides a repeatable evaluation pipeline.

🔍 Overview

  • Agents are non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different outputs and execution paths.
  • Changes to prompts, tool descriptions, retrieval settings, or memory configuration can alter behavior in ways that a text review alone can’t reveal.
  • Model endpoints, knowledge bases, and external APIs can change independently of the repository and affect agent behavior.

🧩 Agent Development Lifecycle

  • One lifecycle, two loops, and a single explicit standard for judging every change.
  • Every prompt, tool, retrieval, and memory change is versioned with an evaluation attached, and the lineage is kept.
  • Run each example k times. Judge on pass rate and failure distribution.
  • Re‑run the standard on a schedule and alert on deviations from the baseline.

⚙️ Evaluation Method

  • Gold standard means one specific artifact: the bundle of verifiable criteria, their thresholds, and the approved examples they are checked against.
  • Metrics used:
    • Groundedness: Decompose the answer into claims and check each against the retrieved sources.
    • Chunk‑level source precision: Is each retrieved chunk, as a whole, necessary for this question?
    • Fact‑level source precision: Decompose each chunk into individual facts and check whether each fact is necessary.
    • Retrieval coverage: For each sub‑question, does any retrieved chunk answer it?
    • Response precision: Of the claims in the answer, how many are necessary?
  • Sample results:
    Metric Question 1 Question 2 Question 3
    Chunk‑level precision 1.00 1.00 1.00
    Fact‑level precision 0.59 0.53 0.09

🚀 Reference Implementation

  • Built a reference implementation: an internal policy assistant answering HR policy questions over a document knowledge base.
  • The accompanying AWS Samples repository includes:
    • Infrastructure deployment
    • The HR agent
    • Custom evaluators
    • Scripts for baseline evaluation and prompt‑change re‑evaluation (09-run-eval.sh and 10-optimize-prompt.sh)
    • Optional checks for judge repeatability, model comparison, cost, and latency.

💡 Impact of a Prompt Change

  • Changed exactly one thing: the system prompt.
  • Added three constraints: ground strictly in retrieved content, ignore irrelevant retrieved content, and keep answers focused.
  • The agent, knowledge base, evaluators, and questions were untouched, so the before‑and‑after differs by one variable.
  • The first question improved substantially.
  • Measures a single sample of a distribution; behavior can’t be read off the text of a prompt.
  • Doesn’t fire because nothing in your repository changed.
  • Passes and fails for reasons unrelated to your change.

📈 Why It Matters

  • Non‑deterministic behavior and external changes make text‑only reviews insufficient.
  • Systematic versioning, automated evaluation, and scheduled re‑evaluation provide a reliable way to maintain agent quality as components evolve.

#LLM #AIagents #Evaluation #EnterpriseAI

Source: From prototype to production: Engineering agents with Agent DLC | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Amazon Bedrock adds new models and AgentCore upgrades
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock adds new models and AgentCore upgrades

Amazon Bedrock announced a set of updates that add new large‑language models, expand AgentCore tooling, and improve pricing and performance across its AI services.

🔍 Overview

  • Amazon Bedrock now provides access to leading models and the tools to build and scale AI applications securely.
  • The platform is extended with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for building, connecting, and optimizing agents.

🤖 New Models

  • Claude Haiku 5.5 – built for subagents and high‑volume, cost‑sensitive work; 75 % cheaper than Claude Haiku 4.5; first Haiku with effort controls to tune cost against intelligence.
  • OpenAI GPT‑6.1 Terra – generally available; matches GPT‑6 Astra on the Agents’ Last Exam and completes tasks >3 × faster than GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol; token prices ≥50 % lower than GPT‑6.1 Sol and GPT‑5.6 Terra; accepts text and images up to 1 million tokens; Ultrafast mode for real‑time coding assistants.
  • Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic – speech‑to‑speech model that improves reasoning, instruction following, and tool‑calling accuracy; lower latency at the same price as Amazon Nova 2.
  • GLM 5.3 (Z.ai) – open‑weight model for agentic coding and long‑horizon software engineering; 1‑million‑token context window and prompt caching; limited to eligible enterprise customers.
  • TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 – converts entire videos into structured, time‑coded metadata; reads visuals, audio, and on‑screen text in a single pass with no separate ingestion pipeline.

📊 Model Highlights

Model Key Highlights
Claude Haiku 5.5 Subagents, 75 % cost reduction vs 4.5, effort controls
GPT‑6.1 Terra >3 × faster than GPT‑6 Astra, ≥50 % cheaper tokens, 1 M token multimodal input
Nova 2.5 Sonic Better reasoning & tool‑calling, lower latency, same price
GLM 5.3 Open‑weight, 1 M token window, prompt caching
Pegasus 1.5 Video‑to‑metadata, single‑pass visual/audio/text analysis

⚙️ AgentCore Enhancements

  • AgentCore CLI v1.0 GA: faster startup, consistent command structure, supports more resources; existing projects upgrade with a single command.
  • AgentCore Gateway now supports Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel APIs and model fallback; can route requests to alternate models when the primary is throttled or unreachable; includes a circuit‑breaker and VPC private‑target support.
  • Integration with AWS Step Functions allows agents to invoke Standard or Express workflows as tools; the agent decides when to run a workflow and Step Functions executes each step as defined.

💰 Pricing & Performance

  • Claude Haiku 5.5 costs around 75 % less than Claude Haiku 4.5.
  • GPT‑6.1 Terra token prices are at least 50 % lower than GPT‑6.1 Sol and GPT‑5.6 Terra.
  • Nova 2.5 Sonic offers lower latency at the same price as Nova 2.

🚀 Availability

  • Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT‑5.6 models with cross‑Region inference, and Daybreak Red (security‑focused model) are now in AWS GovCloud (US) and AWS GovCloud (US‑East) for eligible customers.
  • GLM 5.3 is available to eligible enterprise customers.
  • Structured outputs (schema‑compliant JSON) are now available for all Claude models on Amazon Bedrock.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Faster, cheaper, and higher‑capacity models enable more extensive AI workloads such as large‑scale agent orchestration, multimodal content creation, and real‑time assistance.
  • AgentCore’s new CLI, Gateway, and Step Functions integration simplify building production‑grade AI agents that can fail‑over between models and operate securely within VPCs.
  • Structured JSON outputs reduce integration effort, allowing developers to consume model responses without custom parsing or retries.

#AmazonBedrock #AIModels #AgentCore #Claude #OpenAI

Source: ICYMI: What landed for AI builders in October 2026 | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore adds Web Search API
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore adds Web Search API

Amazon announced a new Web Search API on Bedrock AgentCore that lets developers retrieve ranked web results with a single API call.

🔍 Overview

  • The Web Search API returns ranked results from an Amazon‑operated web index.
  • Each result includes a text extract and, when available, the page title, URL, and publication time.
  • The API can be invoked via AWS SDKs or the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI).

🧩 How it works

  • The API is exposed as the InvokeWebSearch operation on the bedrock-agentcore data plane.
  • It runs on the same search infrastructure that powers Alexa+, Kiro, Quick, and other Amazon products.
  • Calls are signed with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) using standard IAM credentials; no separate API key is required.
  • The recommended integration point for most agentic workloads is the AgentCore Gateway, which provides a single Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint that combines web search with other tools.
  • When executed from a VPC, the call can travel through an interface VPC endpoint.

⚙️ Key details

  • Result limits: Request between 1 and 25 results per query; if maxResults is omitted, up to 25 results are returned.
  • Result content: Each result contains a text extract and, when available, title, URL, and publication time.
  • Search query: searchQuery may be up to 200 characters.
  • Domain filtering: Include or exclude up to 100 domain names; a root domain also matches its subdomains.
  • Publication‑time filtering: Use publishedAfter and publishedBefore (RFC 3339 UTC) to restrict results; both bounds are inclusive.
  • Permissions: The caller must have the IAM permission bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch on the managed web search tool. One IAM policy covers both the gateway and direct API routes.
  • Execution context: If code runs on AWS Lambda, Amazon ECS, Amazon EC2, or Amazon EKS, the execution role supplies credentials automatically.
Component Description
Operation InvokeWebSearch on the bedrock-agentcore data plane
Endpoint AgentCore Gateway MCP endpoint (recommended)
Permission bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch IAM permission

🚀 Availability

  • The API can be called from any environment that can use the AWS SDKs or AWS CLI.
  • Calls are signed with the same IAM credentials used for other AWS services.
  • When run inside a VPC, an interface VPC endpoint can be used for private connectivity.
  • Execution roles for Lambda, ECS, EC2, and EKS automatically provide the necessary credentials.

💡 Why it matters

  • Provides a direct, compliant web‑search capability for agents without managing external API keys.
  • Leverages Amazon’s own high‑quality search infrastructure, ensuring consistent quality and compliance.
  • Integrates seamlessly with other AgentCore tools such as AgentCore Browser through the same endpoint.
  • Enables developers to scope searches to trusted domains and recent publications, improving relevance for AI‑driven applications.

#AmazonWebServices #Bedrock #WebSearchAPI

Source: Introducing the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore enhances AI agent evaluation with new metrics and custom tools
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore enhances AI agent evaluation with new metrics and custom tools

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore has introduced expanded evaluation capabilities for AI agents, combining built-in, third-party, and customizable metrics to assess performance across multiple dimensions. This update provides developers with a comprehensive toolkit to measure agent effectiveness at both granular and conversational levels.

🔍 Overview

AgentCore now integrates three evaluator types: AWS-authored built-in evaluators, third-party managed evaluators from DeepEval/AutoEval, and custom derivations. These tools assess agent behaviors through:

  • Trace-level metrics: Per-turn or per-tool-call analysis
  • Session-level metrics: Holistic conversation outcomes

🧩 How it works

  • Built-in evaluators (e.g., Builtin.GoalSuccessRate, Builtin.Helpfulness) are pre-configured by AWS and referenced by ID.
  • Third-party managed evaluators leverage DeepEval/AutoEval libraries, with AgentCore handling hosting and inference.
  • Custom evaluators modify existing evaluators’ models, prompts, or rubrics while retaining standard usage.

⚙️ Key details

The system covers 18+ evaluation dimensions across five categories:

Category Evaluators
Task Completion GoalSuccessRate, ToolSelectionAccuracy, ToolParameterAccuracy
Skills SkillSelectionAccuracy, SkillInstructionFollowing
Safety Harmfulness, Stereotyping, Security
Conversation ConversationCompleteness, KnowledgeRetention, Possible
Trajectory TrajectoryExactOrderMatch, TrajectoryInOrderMatch, TrajectoryAnyOrderMatch

Additional specialized metrics include Humor for consumer agents.

💡 Why it matters

  • Reliability: Built-in evaluators are AWS-benchmarked for common use cases.
  • Flexibility: Third-party integration allows reuse of existing development metrics in production.
  • Customization: Developers can create domain-specific evaluators without starting from scratch.
  • Comprehensive coverage: Metrics span tool accuracy, safety, long-term context retention, and conversational flow.

#AIagents #AmazonBedrock #EvaluationTools #LLM #AutoEval #DeepEval

Source: The agent evaluation playbook: Built-in, DeepEval, and AutoEval on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations | Amazon Web Services

item.title: AWS Quick powers an AI‑driven product development lifecycle with human approval
item.description:
AWS Quick powers an AI‑driven product development lifecycle with human approval

AI‑PDLC (AI‑Driven Product Development Lifecycle) shows how enterprises can accelerate product creation by stitching together fragmented knowledge sources with AWS Quick agents and keeping a human in the loop.

🔍 Overview

The AI‑PDLC framework strings together six specialist agents built on AWS Quick, an Orchestrator that guides a single conversation, and coding agents accessed via the open Agent Client Protocol (ACP). At every stage a human approval gate must be satisfied, and all artifacts are stored in a shared space that ties decisions back to their source data.

🧩 How it works

  • Enterprise connectors pull context from Slack, Outlook, Jira, Salesforce, SharePoint, ServiceNow, and many other sources.
  • AWS Quick builds a personal knowledge graph that links people, projects, and decisions across those tools.
  • The Orchestrator reads each specialist’s question framework at runtime, asks targeted questions, and dispatches artifact generation to the appropriate agent.
  • A single conversation drives the entire journey; the pipeline advances only after human approval at each step.
  • All generated artifacts land in a common markdown file (prototype_spec.md) that contains acceptance criteria, personas, screens, and data model, with every decision traceable to its source.

⚙️ Six specialist agents

Agent Responsibility
Discovery Guides structured pain‑point analysis via Q&A, URL ingestion, and direct pulls from Slack, Jira, support tickets, Salesforce, and research repositories; scores pain points and produces a Pain Point Board.
Prioritize Scores each use case on two transparent 0–10 frameworks (LLM capability match, tool availability, user acceptance or feasibility, business impact, effort); generates a Scoring Matrix that can be opened to trace why one use case outranks another.
Working Backwards Generates a full PR/FAQ using the Amazon Working Backwards method, adding customer and internal FAQs covering unit economics, failure modes, regulatory risk, and competitive landscape.
Spec Generator (Implicit in the workflow) consolidates output into prototype_spec.md.
Designer (Implicit) creates design artifacts that flow into the specification.
Orchestrator Leads the conversation, reads specialist frameworks, asks targeted questions, and routes artifact creation; presents human‑approval prompts before advancing.

📈 End‑to‑End lifecycle

The AI‑PDLC spans eight phases, with the first four handled by the six AWS Quick agents and the last four by coding agents such as Kiro:

  • Discover – Discovery agent collects and scores pain points.
  • Decide – Prioritize agent ranks use cases.
  • Design – Working Backwards and Designer agents produce PR/FAQ and design artifacts.
  • Prototype – Spec Generator consolidates into a prototype specification.
  • Engineer – Coding agents (e.g., Kiro, Claude Code) build from the specification via ACP.
  • Ship – Coding agents deliver the product.
  • Operate – Production data flows back into Discovery, closing the loop.
  • Learn – Continuous improvement driven by new signals.

🛠️ Coding agents & ACP

  • AWS Quick can delegate development tasks to AI coding agents using the Agent Client Protocol (ACP), an open JSON‑RPC 2.0 standard with no vendor lock‑in.
  • Customers may invoke their preferred coding agent—such as Kiro or Claude Code—to build against the specification generated by AI‑PDLC.

✅ Human approval & traceability

  • A human approval gate exists at every stage; the pipeline proceeds only after the gate is cleared.
  • Every decision is linked back to its source data, ensuring full traceability across Slack, Outlook, Jira, Salesforce, SharePoint, ServiceNow, and other enterprise systems.

📊 Consistent evaluation with UAEF

  • The Unified Agent Evaluation Framework (UAEF) provides a framework‑agnostic way to score agents across different SDKs (LangGraph, LangChain, Strands Agents, Bedrock AgentCore).
  • UAEF uses adapters to convert native traces into a canonical AgentTrace, then scores the trace with 36 built‑in metrics across 7 quality dimensions (tool calling, response quality, responsible AI, performance, multi‑turn conversation, multi‑agent coordination, reasoning).
  • Results are stored in Amazon DynamoDB (metadata) and Amazon S3 (full results) and generate reports that help teams detect regressions, understand changes, and close the evaluation‑learn loop.
  • UAEF can invoke an agent given an ARN or HTTP endpoint, collect responses, and adapt them in a single step.

#AWSQuick #AIProductDevelopment #AgentEvaluation #EnterpriseAI

Source: Accelerating product development with AI-driven lifecycle management (AI-PDLC) in AWS Quick | Amazon Web Services Source: UAEF: A framework-agnostic system for closed-loop evaluation of AI agents | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Microsoft discovers “Lazarus” backdoor that reprograms dormant neurons in AI agents
item.description:
Microsoft discovers “Lazarus” backdoor that reprograms dormant neurons in AI agents

Microsoft researchers have identified a new backdoor technique, dubbed “Lazarus,” that can silently reprogram a handful of dormant neurons in a large language model, enabling an otherwise normal AI agent to execute malicious commands when a hidden trigger fires.

🔍 Overview

  • “Lazarus” can reprogram fewer than 10 dormant neurons in an LLM without any additional training.
  • The altered model passes standard safety evaluations and behaves normally until a trigger appears.
  • A trigger can be as simple as a date change (e.g., the clock passing midnight into 2027) that causes the agent to download and run attacker code.
  • The technique is especially serious for AI agents that have tool or terminal access.

🧩 How it works

  • The backdoor edits the model’s weight matrix directly, targeting dormant neurons that rarely affect ordinary outputs.
  • Because the change is tiny, it does not affect benchmark performance, allowing the model to clear typical safety tests.
  • When the hidden trigger is observed, the agent executes the malicious payload with whatever permissions the user has granted it.

⚠️ Risks

  • Silent download and execution of attacker‑supplied code.
  • Theft of secrets accessible to the agent.
  • Execution of destructive commands while still appearing safe in evaluations.
  • Large attack surface inherent to AI agents that can invoke external tools.

🛡️ Defenses

  • Microsoft Foundry verifies model provenance, ties each model to a trusted publisher, and scans the surrounding software environment before onboarding open‑weight models.
  • Models are run inside Microsoft‑controlled containers that are separately scanned for critical vulnerabilities.
  • Ongoing development of:
    • AI‑powered weight scanning.
    • Red‑team tools for detecting anomalous model modifications.
    • Cryptographic model signing with tamper‑evident provenance and audit trails.
  • Frontier agents can be asked to spot anomalous weight modifications, providing an additional detection signal.
Defense Mechanism Description
Weight Scanning Uses AI to analyze model weights for unexpected changes.
Red‑Team Harness Internal tools that probe models for hidden backdoors.
Cryptographic Signing Adds verifiable provenance and tamper‑proof audit trails to model files.

🚦 Detection limits

  • No scan can prove beyond any doubt that a model is safe.
  • Reliable detection requires diff‑ing against the original, unmodified weights, making provenance critical.
  • Even with strong provenance, risk remains if a trusted provider is compromised (e.g., through its training infrastructure or an insider).

📅 Outlook

  • Microsoft is turning detection techniques into a red‑team harness and exploring weight‑scanning signals for open‑weight model onboarding.
  • Plans are underway to require cryptographic signing of models with verifiable provenance.
  • The research began as a quick experiment in March, where Claude Code with Opus 4.5 was asked to hard‑wire a few activations without training—and succeeded.
  • Ongoing collaboration between researchers and security teams aims to translate these findings into product defenses and guidance that keep customers protected.

#AIsecurity #ModelProvenance #Backdoor #MicrosoftFoundry

Source: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents - Microsoft Research

item.title: AWS Quick Launches Enterprise AI Workspace for Task Automation and Data Analysis

AWS Quick Launches Enterprise AI Workspace for Task Automation and Data Analysis

AWS Quick is an AI-powered workspace designed for knowledge workers to automate tasks, analyze data, build web applications, and conduct research using natural language and AI agents.

item.title: eBay Restricts Access for Third-Party AI Agents Including Meta Muse
item.description:
eBay Restricts Access for Third-Party AI Agents Including Meta Muse

eBay appears to have blocked third-party AI agents, including Meta’s Muse, from browsing its platform. While technology companies tout AI agents to find deals, book travel, and buy goods, retailers and service providers continue to block or restrict automated agents from accessing their sites.

🔍 Overview

Until recently, agents like Meta’s Muse were able to browse eBay to pull listings, links, prices, shipping details, and condition notes for users. Over the weekend, Muse was unable to extract details from eBay, stating it was blocked from the site. The Verge re-created the experience using other search queries and found Muse directed users to outside sites mirroring eBay listings.

eBay previously updated its user agreement to ban tools like “buy-for-me agents” and “LLM-driven bots” that place orders without human review. Responding to inquiries about third-party limits, eBay spokesperson Sybille St. Arromand stated:

“As it pertains to third-parties, we take a selective approach to how they access and interact with our marketplace. We have restricted agent access in certain cases, including unauthorized scraping and training on our data.”

St. Arromand added that eBay is having ongoing discussions with potential partners to evaluate ways third-party agents could help customers discover inventory while preserving its end-to-end marketplace experience. Meta declined to comment.

⚙️ Retailer Approaches to AI Agents

Retailers have demonstrated varying levels of comfort regarding third-party AI agent access:

Retailer / Platform Access Level Details
Amazon Fully Blocked Blocks external agents entirely from browsing or shopping.
eBay Restricted Bans automated purchasing bots; restricted browsing agents like Muse for unauthorized scraping and training.
Target Partially Restricted Allows agents to successfully browse in some instances while blocking them in others.
Shopify Open Opened its catalog of a billion listings for shoppers to set up agents to purchase items on their behalf.

💡 Challenges and Adoption Rates

Integrating AI agents into e-commerce presents operational friction because retail sites are designed for human limitations rather than bot swarms. In October, The Verge found that Muse could be used to hold listings hostage on consignment site The RealReal by continually adding products to a cart, prompting The RealReal to update its bot system.

Furthermore, current consumer usage of third-party AI shopping agents remains minimal:

  • Uber: Fulfilled only 4 rides via third-party agents in Q3 and around 500 Uber Eats orders during Halloween week.
  • DoorDash: Fulfilled only “several hundred” orders via third-party agents out of 993 million total quarterly orders.

#ECommerce #AIAgents #eBay #Meta #TechNews

Source: eBay appears to have shut the door on third-party AI agents

item.title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL Added to Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
item.description:
NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL Added to Amazon SageMaker JumpStart

Today NVIDIA announced that the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL vision‑language model is now available through Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. The model can be deployed in SageMaker Studio with a few steps or with a few lines of the SageMaker Python SDK.

🔍 Overview

  • Super VL is the vision‑language model (VLM) in the NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 family.
  • Inputs: images, video, and text.
  • Output: generated text.
  • Designed for document intelligence, GUI understanding for computer‑use agents, video question answering, and multimodal agentic applications.

🧩 Architecture

  • Language backbone: 120 B‑parameter hybrid Mixture‑of‑Experts (MoE) model with 12 B active parameters per token.
    • 88 layers interleaving Mamba‑2 and MoE layers (512 routed experts, 22 active per token) plus 8 attention layers.
    • Initialized from Nemotron 3 Super Base and distilled from Nemotron 3 Ultra Base.
  • Vision encoder: C‑RADIO encoder that processes images and sampled video frames.
  • Vision‑language connector: Maps encoder outputs into the language backbone’s embedding space.
  • Both encoder and connector remain in BF16 for all variants.
  • Supports context lengths up to 1 million tokens and includes a built‑in Multi‑Token Prediction (MTP) head for speculative decoding (not enabled in the default JumpStart serving configuration for NVFP4).

⚙️ Key Details

  • Reasoning: Enabled by default; can be toggled per request with enable_thinking.
  • Languages supported: English, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Spanish, Chinese.
  • Outputs: Tool calling, JSON schema output, configurable reasoning.
  • License: OpenMDW License Agreement, version 1.1.
  • Training pipeline:
    • Continued pre‑training → long‑context & software‑engineering mid‑training → vision‑language training.
    • Two‑stage multimodal supervised fine‑tuning on vision, reasoning, code, tool, chat, safety, and long‑context data.
    • Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and human feedback (NeMo RL, NeMo Gym), multi‑teacher on‑policy distillation, and final MTP‑head training.

📦 Variants

Variant Precision Checkpoint Size Quantization
NVFP4 4‑bit weights & activations (W4A4) on Blackwell GPUs; vision encoder, connector, Mamba convolutions, embeddings in BF16; MoE router in FP32 ~75 GB Quantized from BF16 with quantization‑aware distillation
BF16 Full‑precision BF16 weights ~249 GB Reference weights

🚀 Availability

  • Deployment: One‑click launch from SageMaker JumpStart; deployable via SageMaker Studio UI or SageMaker Python SDK.
  • Instance types:
    Instance Recommended for
    ml.g7.24xlarge Default
    ml.g7.48xlarge NVFP4 variant
    ml.p5en.48xlarge BF16 variant

💡 Why It Matters

  • Targets agentic workloads that must both see and read.
  • Enables vision‑language agents that combine reasoning, coding, tool use, document understanding, and video understanding.
  • Provides large‑context (up to 1 M tokens) and built‑in speculative decoding to accelerate generation.

#NVIDIA #SageMaker #VisionLanguage #AIagents

Source: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart | Amazon Web Services

item.title: NVIDIA Upstreams Agent Substrate and Introduces Snapshot, NVKE, and NVKR
item.description:
NVIDIA Upstreams Agent Substrate and Introduces Snapshot, NVKE, and NVKR

NVIDIA is contributing upstream to Agent Substrate—an open-source agent runtime donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox—while introducing NVIDIA Snapshot, NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE), and NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR) as part of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform.

🔍 Overview

Agent Substrate, NVIDIA Snapshot, NVKE, and NVKR address infrastructure needs across AI agent session management, GPU workload startup times, and managed Kubernetes cluster operations.

Component Description Status / License
Agent Substrate Security-hardened runtime that multiplexes sandboxed agent sessions over worker Pods Donated to CNCF Sandbox
NVIDIA Snapshot Checkpoint and restore system for GPU workloads on Kubernetes Open-source (DSX AI Factory)
NVKE Software to run managed Kubernetes clusters on factory infrastructure Apache 2.0 (Public Preview)
NVKR Reproducible builds for OS images, container images, and Helm charts Apache 2.0 (Public Preview)

🧩 How Agent Substrate Works

Agent Substrate provides a security-hardened, zero-trust runtime engineered to run agents and tools with 10x higher density than standard containers by decoupling actor state from worker Pods:

  • Session Multiplexing: Idle sessions are snapshotted out of gVisor or microVM sandboxes—including memory and filesystem state—freeing the underlying worker Pod.
  • Bypassing Control Plane Latency: Restoring an actor onto a free worker Pod skips API server, admission, etcd, scheduler, and kubelet roundtrips.
  • Kubernetes Integration: Worker Pods remain standard Kubernetes Pods, ensuring cluster scheduling, placement policies, and quotas continue to apply.
  • Upstream Capabilities: Public developments include router request parking (#221), request line protection for running actors (#1229), and Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) device pluggability (#752), with NVIDIA GPUs designated as the first supported device.

⚡ NVIDIA Snapshot GPU Checkpoint and Restore

NVIDIA Snapshot eliminates repeated workload initialization by saving fully initialized CPU and GPU memory states into portable artifacts:

  • Operations: Checkpointing is managed via PodSnapshot or SnapshotJob custom resources, while restoration uses the nvidia.com/restore-from Pod annotation.
  • Workload Compatibility: Features examples for vLLM, SGLang, and NVIDIA TensorRT LLM, and supports single-node multi-GPU workloads across tensor parallelism (TP), data and expert parallelism (DEP), and decode context parallelism (DCP).
  • Restoration Speed: Across tested configurations, Snapshot restores replicas in 3.6 to 42.7 seconds—8x to 36x faster than cold starts. Crusoe reduced GLM-5.3 Pod readiness from ~8 minutes to 31 seconds on NVIDIA HGX B300, while Saturn Cloud cut vLLM startup from 2–8.5 minutes to 6–34 seconds.

🛠️ NVKE and NVKR Infrastructure Tools

NVKE and NVKR allow AI factories to construct and operate managed Kubernetes services:

  • NVKR (NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes): Builds validated operating system images, container images, binaries, and Helm charts based on specific GPU generations and software versions.
  • NVKE (NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine): Deploys management and workload clusters using artifacts produced by NVKR, leveraging Cluster API infrastructure provider CAPNICo and NVIDIA Infra Controller (NICo).
  • Node Identity & Observability: Requires nodes to present an attested SPIFFE identity before receiving join credentials, and exports telemetry via an OpenTelemetry-based Helm chart over OTLP.
  • Certification: NVKE is a Certified Kubernetes AI Platform and Certified Kubernetes Installer tested on Kubernetes 1.36.

#Kubernetes #NVIDIA #AIAgents #GPUInfrastructure #CloudNative

Source: Agent Substrate: Advancing Kubernetes for Agents at Scale | NVIDIA Technical Blog Source: Start and Restore GPU Workloads in Seconds with NVIDIA Snapshot | NVIDIA Technical Blog Source: Manage Kubernetes Clusters for GPU Infrastructure with NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: Managing AI-Generated Pull Request Descriptions with HTML Details and Summary Tags
item.description:
Managing AI-Generated Pull Request Descriptions with HTML Details and Summary Tags

Developers are increasingly utilizing coding agents like Claude Code and Codex to open pull requests (PRs) and manage project changes. While these agents generate accurate and comprehensive descriptions—detailing the problem, the solution, and verification steps—the volume of text can be overwhelming, leading to the use of specific Markdown techniques to organize information for human reviewers.

🧩 How it works

GitHub Markdown supports the HTML <details><summary> elements, which render as a collapsed heading that can be expanded to view larger blocks of text. This feature allows developers to bundle agent-written content behind a concise, human-curated summary:

  • The <summary> tag serves as the clickable line of text that acts as a summary.
  • The <details> element wraps the rest of the content to keep it hidden until expanded.
  • A carefully selected opening paragraph provides a high-level explanation to get readers up to speed.
  • The full agent-written description is placed within the tags to prevent the reader’s eyes from glazing over.
  • Screenshots are sometimes included to quickly illustrate new features.

⚙️ Key details

To maintain clarity, the order of the tags can be remembered using the five-syllable mnemonic “details-summary.” Developers use the summary line to identify the source and intensity of the AI work.

Attribute Usage in PR Summary
Model Name Identifies the specific agent used, such as Claude Opus 5.5.
Effort Level Indicates the intensity of the work, such as “Medium”.
Human Judgement Used to select the short opener or extract a summary from the agent’s text.

💡 Why it matters

Using the <details><summary> structure ensures that the PR remains a functional unit of work for bundling commits and documenting decisions without sacrificing readability. It provides a promise to the reader that the visible text represents human judgment on what is worth their time, while keeping the exhaustive agent-generated verification steps and data accessible for those who need it.

#GitHub #AIagents #ClaudeCode #Markdown #PullRequests

Source: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind

item.title: OpenHands Cloud Introduces Scheduled and Event-Driven Automation Execution Service
item.description:
OpenHands Cloud Introduces Scheduled and Event-Driven Automation Execution Service

A new automation execution service has been developed for OpenHands Cloud, providing support for both scheduled and event-driven automation workflows.

🔍 Overview

The Automation Service allows users to manage and execute agent workflows based on predefined schedules or external triggers. Key features include:

  • Scheduled Automations: Run OpenHands conversations on a cron schedule.
  • Event-Driven Automations: Trigger automations via webhooks, such as GitHub events.
  • API Key Management: Per-user API keys for secure automation access.
  • Run History: Track automation runs with status and results.

🧩 How it works

System responsibilities are divided across several components:

  • Automation Service: Owns automation definitions, cron scheduling, webhooks, run history, dispatch, and sandbox lifecycle orchestration.
  • Agent Server and OpenHands/software-agent-sdk: Execute agent conversations and own agent/tool behavior, workspaces, events, and API endpoints.
  • OpenHands/typescript-client: Provides typed browser access to the Agent Server API.
  • OpenHands/OpenHands: Owns the Agent Canvas UI and frontend integration.

The codebase is structured into specific modules:

File Description
app.py FastAPI application entry point
router.py API routes for CRUD operations
scheduler.py Background scheduler for cron jobs
dispatcher.py Dispatches pending runs to OpenHands
models.py SQLAlchemy models
schemas.py Pydantic schemas for API

⚙️ Key details

The service is built using Python 3.12+ and uses uv for dependency management. For storage, it utilizes PostgreSQL, with testcontainers available for testing.

Database migration and creation rules include:

  • SQLite databases are migrated on startup.
  • PostgreSQL databases are not migrated on startup unless AUTOMATION_RUN_MIGRATIONS_ON_STARTUP=true (or 1) is set. When set, each replica runs alembic upgrade head before serving requests, using an advisory lock so concurrent replicas take turns. A failed migration stops the replica from starting.
  • Setting AUTOMATION_CREATE_DATABASE_IF_MISSING=true (or 1) instructs migrations to connect to the postgres database and create the target database if missing. This requires the database user to have the CREATEDB privilege.

🚀 Deployment

For local development, dependencies can be installed using uv sync --group dev, and the application can be run with uv run uvicorn openhands.automation.app:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --reload.

Container deployment can be built and run using Docker:

  • docker build -t automation -f containers/Dockerfile .
  • docker run -p 8000:8000 automation

The service is deployed via the deploy repository at https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/deploy. Docker images are automatically built and pushed to ghcr.io/openhands/automation on every push to main and on tags.

#OpenHands #Automation #Python #FastAPI #DevOps

Source: OpenHands/automation

item.title: Open-source Hive runtime enables parallel AI agent colonies for business tasks
item.description:
Open-source Hive runtime enables parallel AI agent colonies for business tasks

Hive has been updated as an open-source runtime for colonies of AI agents designed to perform real business work. The system coordinates “queen” agents that manage parallel workers to complete complex tasks without the need for pre-wired workflow graphs.

🧩 How it works

Hive utilizes a hierarchical structure to manage business workflows as they unfold:

  • Initial Learning: A queen agent performs the first part of a job herself to learn the requirements, then saves the method as a reusable skill.
  • Colony Formation: After defining the method, the queen proposes a colony and assigns the remaining work to as many parallel worker agents as the task needs.
  • Shared Tracking: Every result is written to a shared tracker—a SQLite table on disk—rather than a context window. This allows the system to query, audit, and resume work.
  • Active Auditing: The queen checks every row of the tracker for accuracy. For example, in a research task, a queen can identify and clear incorrect entries recorded by workers before providing a final answer.

🔍 Overview

Queens are long-lived agents with specific roles, memory, and tools. Because the system shapes the colony dynamically, there is no fixed workflow graph to draw. The state of the work is maintained on disk, keeping track of what has been completed and what remains.

⚙️ Key details

The platform is designed to be compatible with a wide range of models and local configurations:

Feature Supported Options
LLM Providers Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini, Groq, Cerebras, OpenRouter, Hive LLM
Local Models Ollama (requires no API key)
Security API keys stored encrypted under ~/.hive
Tools Quickstart installs uv and ripgrep if missing

🚀 Availability

Setting up Hive requires Python 3.11+, Node.js 20+, and git.

  • Installation: Users can run pip install "aden-hive[tools]" to install the runtime from PyPI.
  • Management: The command hive open builds and opens the dashboard at http://127.0.0.1:8787.
  • Development: Projects can be built on Hive’s agent loop by depending on the aden-hive package. Optional packages are also available for features such as chat-app channels.

#AIagents #OpenSource #Automation #Python #SoftwareDevelopment

Source: aden-hive/hive

item.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Integrates with Okta Cross App Access for Secure Agent Governance
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Integrates with Okta Cross App Access for Secure Agent Governance

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale using any framework or model. A new integration with Okta Cross App Access (XAA) allows organizations to manage agent identity and governance directly within their identity provider (IdP).

🔍 Overview

This solution establishes a clear separation between governance and execution. Okta serves as the governance plane, deciding which agent may act for which user against specific resources. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore serves as the execution plane, managing credentials and turning governance decisions into valid access tokens.

Component Role
Okta Governance plane: decides which agent acts for which user against which resource.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity Execution plane: holds credentials and redeems grants for tokens in a vault.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime Validates Okta’s grant.

🧩 How it works

The identity flow ensures that agent actions are always tied to a verified user session:

  • User Sign-in: Users access a backend for frontend (BFF) using OpenID Connect via the agent’s linked Okta app.
  • Token Exchange: For each request, the BFF performs an RFC 8693 token exchange, trading the user’s ID token for an Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) at Okta’s authorization server.
  • Okta Verification: Okta checks that the agent is active, the user is assigned to it, and an administrator has approved the applications and scopes the agent might reach.
  • Execution: The BFF invokes the agent on the AgentCore runtime using the ID-JAG. AgentCore Identity then redeems the ID-JAG for a short-lived access token accepted by the resource.

⚙️ Key details

The system utilizes three distinct tokens to record different decisions throughout the request lifecycle:

  • ID Token: Identifies the user.
  • Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG): Represents Okta’s decision; single-use and expires in 5 minutes.
  • Access Token: Issued by Okta’s custom authorization server, naming both the user and the agent.

In testing, the governance process proved highly responsive. When an administrator removed a user’s assignment, Okta refused new agent requests for that user within approximately 1 second. Existing tokens expired within 5 minutes. Performance testing showed that AgentCore Identity added roughly 0.6 seconds of latency to a request taking 30 seconds end to end.

🚀 Availability

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore charges based on usage. A technical walkthrough for building a task agent with this governance model takes about 1 hour. The associated sample code is provided for non-production use, and organizations should consult with security and legal teams before deployment.

#AWS #AmazonBedrock #Okta #AIagents #Cybersecurity

Source: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 1 | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Amazon Quick defines a four‑question taxonomy for AI agents and triggers
item.description:
Amazon Quick defines a four‑question taxonomy for AI agents and triggers

Over the past year, Amazon Quick’s agents have moved from answering questions to taking actions such as scheduling meetings, running research, and generating reports.

🔍 Taxonomy

  • The taxonomy decomposes agentic work into four plain questions: When?, What?, Who?, and How?
  • When and What are carried by a trigger that starts the work and describes the task.
  • Who is the agent that takes on the trigger.
  • How is the set of capabilities (tools, skills, and workflows) the agent uses to perform the task.

⚙️ Triggers

  • Human‑initiated – a person opens a conversation and asks the agent to do something.
  • Agent‑delegated – one agent, mid‑task, invokes another to handle a sub‑problem.
  • Scheduled – time‑based activation, e.g., “run financial research every Monday at 9 am.”
  • Event‑driven – a signal from an external system such as a new email, a Slack mention, a file change, or a webhook.
  • The trigger type influences execution style; a scheduled background task may stay conservative (do nothing if uncertain), while a human‑initiated trigger is responsive (ask rather than stop).

🤖 Agents

  • An agent is defined as a persistent, learning actor.
  • Two agents given identical input can differ because they carry different instructions, capabilities, and histories.
  • The agent is the entity that interprets instructions; it is not the instructions themselves.
  • Instructions are standing guidance that defines persona, role, context files, and operating principles.
  • Everything else (LLM model, conversation history, triggers) is considered extrinsic and can be swapped without changing the agent.

🛠️ Capabilities

Capability Description
Tools Atomic operations with a typed schema (e.g., send an email, query a database, read a file). The caller sees a uniform interface: name, description, parameters, result.
Skills Structured guidance with room for judgment; includes instructions plus resources (templates, scripts, examples). Loaded through progressive disclosure, allowing deep expertise without constant cost.
Workflows Deterministic coordination of declared steps, control flow, branching, and error handling. Decision logic resides in code, not model inference. Example: a purchase‑approval route (budget check → manager sign‑off → finance) with fixed order but agent judgment inside each step.
  • Capabilities span a spectrum from fully agentic to fully deterministic.
  • They are updated dynamically; for example, a charting library can be added in one session and removed the next.
  • Learned context is memory that accumulates through use, such as queries that work for a tool, user‑preferred formatting, and edge cases they care about.

📚 Why it matters

  • A request like “I want an agent that monitors my Slack and sends a digest every morning” is typically satisfied by adding a trigger to an existing agent rather than creating a new agent or workflow.
  • This approach keeps the system modular: triggers activate work, agents interpret and act, and capabilities provide the concrete means.

#Amazon #AIAgents #Automation #LLM #AgenticAI

Source: Taxonomy of agentic primitives in Amazon Quick | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Taxbit launches Assist, a permission‑aware AI assistant for compliance teams
item.description:
Taxbit launches Assist, a permission‑aware AI assistant for compliance teams

Taxbit, the digital‑asset tax and accounting compliance platform founded in 2018, has added a cited, permission‑aware AI assistant – Taxbit Assist – directly inside its product dashboard. The assistant helps compliance teams answer questions without digging through documentation or opening support tickets.

🔍 Overview

  • Taxbit serves enterprises such as exchanges, payment services, and brokers.
  • Assist answers questions in‑context, providing source links and indicating when it does not know an answer.
  • More than 55 % of users who ask Assist a question return within 24 hours to ask another, according to internal production analytics.

🧩 How it works

  1. User query – A user types a question in the Taxbit dashboard.
  2. Secure forwarding – A streaming chat API forwards the query to the AgentCore runtime together with the user’s verified identity (email, organization ID, dashboard roles).
  3. Guardrails & PII masking – Amazon Bedrock Guardrails screen the message; any personally identifiable information is masked in place. If the message is blocked, the model is never invoked.
  4. Retrieval – The agent pulls candidate passages from an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base (RAG capability backed by Amazon S3 Vectors) and reranks them server‑side.
  5. Reasoning & permission check – Amazon Bedrock models reason over the passages and verify the user’s feature and role access before recommending any workflow.
  6. Response – The answer streams back to the dashboard with source links; AgentCore memory preserves context across turns.
  7. Observability – Each request emits OpenTelemetry traces to Amazon CloudWatch for evaluation tooling.

⚙️ Key technical details

  • Agent: Small Python application (system prompt, model, eight tools).
  • Runtime: Strands Agents SDK on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
  • Deployment: ARM64 container image stored in Amazon ECR, pulled and scaled on demand.
  • Model access: Runs a foundation model via Amazon Bedrock, using cross‑Region inference profiles and geography‑aware inference for data residency.
  • Security model:
    • The model never receives identity information; email, org ID, and roles are bound to tools before the model sees them.
    • The model can decide whether to check permissions but cannot set whose permissions to check.
    • Input is sanitized at the boundary, preventing prompt‑injection attacks.
  • Data access: The agent has no read access to customer tax data; it answers only from product knowledge and can only create the caller’s own support tickets.
  • Compliance: Developed and operated in line with ISO/IEC 42001, the international standard for AI management systems.

🚀 Availability

Assist is available as an integrated feature inside the Taxbit dashboard for all existing Taxbit customers.

💡 Why it matters

  • Provides immediate, cited answers, reducing the need for manual documentation searches or support tickets.
  • Embeds robust security and privacy safeguards, ensuring identity data never reaches the language model.
  • Leverages Amazon Bedrock’s managed RAG, guardrails, and observability stack, demonstrating a production‑grade AI integration for regulated financial workflows.

#Taxbit #AIassistants #AmazonBedrock #ComplianceAI

Source: Taxbit Assist: A grounded, role-aware AI agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
