  • Automated reasoning is mathematical logic that checks whether a rule holds in every possible case. (“The technology that goes further is automated reasoning, the mathematical logic that checks whether a rule holds in every possible case.”)
  • It can produce a proof that a rule holds on every path described by a precise system model, or pinpoint the exact case where it fails. (“It can establish that a rule holds on every path covered by a precise description of the system and its assumptions, or uncover the exact case where it fails. That result is a proof.”)
  • The proof is only as good as the underlying rules and assumptions, making the design work before deployment the hardest part. (“It is only as good as the rules and assumptions behind it, which is why the hardest work comes before the agent runs.”)
  • AWS has used automated reasoning in production for over a decade on services such as IAM (handling more than 2.1 billion requests per second), the Nitro Hypervisor, S3 Block Public Access, and the VPC Reachability Analyzer. (“AWS has run automated reasoning in production for more than a decade, from Identity and Access Management (IAM) at more than 2.1 billion requests per second to critical systems like the AWS Nitro Hypervisor, Amazon S3 Block Public Access, and VPC Reachability Analyzer. Now we are bringing it to agents.”)

🛠️ Kiro – Building Agents with Rigor

  • Kiro is an agentic coding system that applies structured, spec‑driven requirements before any code is written. (“Kiro, the agentic coding system, brings rigor and mature engineering practices to the build stage of agents. It turns high‑level intent into structured, spec‑driven requirements and uses automated reasoning to surface contradictions, ambiguities, and gaps before any code is written.”)
  • When a rule can be proven, the agent may act autonomously; when proof does not apply, the framework limits the agent’s access and escalates ambiguous cases to a human. (“Where proof does not apply, limit the agent’s access and actions, evaluate its behavior, and send genuine ambiguity to a person to apply judgment.”)

💡 Why It Matters

  • As agents handle higher‑stakes work such as financial transactions, a single mistake can be increasingly harmful. (“As agents take on higher stakes work, like financial transactions, a wrong action becomes increasingly harmful.”)
  • Organizations need confidence that an AI agent will stay within defined limits even when no one is watching. (“Organizations need the confidence to hand an AI agent important work, knowing it will stay within the limits set, even when no one is watching.”)
  • Traditional safeguards—content filtering, testing, and monitoring—are each necessary but none alone can guarantee correct future behavior. (“Content filtering, testing, and monitoring each serve an important purpose, but none of these capabilities alone can promise an agent will behave correctly the next time it runs.”)
  • By combining scoped intent, identity tracking, runtime bounds, post‑run observation, and automated reasoning, Trust in Depth provides a repeatable, auditable safety net for AI agents.

#AWS #AIAgents #AutomatedReasoning #TrustInDepth

Source: Trust in Depth: Giving agents more autonomy without losing control | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Enables Self‑Learning Intelligent Document Processing
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Enables Self‑Learning Intelligent Document Processing

Document‑related tasks cost organizations $19,732 per information worker each year and cut productivity by 21.3 %. Staff can spend up to 30 % of their time on these tasks, while manual data‑entry error rates range from 1 % to 4 %.

Traditional intelligent document processing (IDP) pipelines rely on static templates, extraction rules, and validation logic that must be created for every document format up front. When a supplier changes an invoice layout, the pipeline breaks. Each new vendor multiplies the maintenance effort, creating a scaling burden for organizations that receive invoices from hundreds of suppliers.

In this update we show how Amazon Bedrock AgentCore can be used to build an agentic IDP system that classifies, extracts, validates, and learns from business documents with minimal human intervention.

🔍 Overview

  • Problem – High labor cost, low productivity, and error‑prone manual data entry for document processing.
  • Solution – Replace static templates with AI agents that automatically generate extraction instructions, validate results, and retain knowledge for future documents.
  • Platform – Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: a platform to build, connect, and optimise agents at scale, with any framework or model.
  • Key benefit – New document formats (e.g., supplier invoices, purchase orders, insurance claims, loan applications) are processed without manual template configuration, often in under 20 minutes of deployment time.

🧩 How it Works

The system coordinates eight specialised agents across two graph‑based workflows on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

  1. Identification workflow
    • Analyzer extracts raw text using Amazon Textract and identifies the document type and sender.
    • Matcher searches for similar documents via vector similarity in Amazon S3 Vectors.
  2. If no match is found
    • Instructions generates extraction prompts.
    • Extractor extracts structured data.
    • Validator checks the data against schemas and business rules in Amazon Aurora DSQL.
    • Instructions Fixer refines prompts and retries when validation fails.
    • Save Instructions persists the successful instructions for reuse.
  3. If a match is found
    • Extractor re‑uses the saved instructions.
    • Troubleshooter fixes extracted data directly if validation fails, without altering the stored instructions.

The workflow is triggered by Amazon EventBridge, which starts a Lambda function that records the job in Amazon DynamoDB and invokes the AgentCore runtime. The runtime orchestrates processing through Strands Agents. All agents access AWS resources securely via machine‑to‑machine credentials managed by AgentCore Identity and Amazon Cognito. Lambda functions become agent‑compatible tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) interface of the AgentCore Gateway.

⚙️ Key Details

Agent Role
Analyzer Extract text with Amazon Textract; identify document type and sender
Matcher Find similar documents using vector similarity in Amazon S3 Vectors
Instructions Generate extraction prompts when no prior instruction exists
Extractor Pull structured data from the document
Validator Verify data against schemas and business rules in Amazon Aurora DSQL
Instructions Fixer Refine prompts and retry extraction on validation failure
Save Instructions Persist successful extraction instructions for future reuse
Troubleshooter Amend extracted data directly if validation fails (no instruction change)

Additional platform capabilities:

  • Agents automatically learn from corrections, building a knowledge base of document formats.
  • Over time, similar documents are processed with minimal additional configuration.
  • Deployment of the full multi‑agent IDP system often completes in under 20 minutes.

🚀 Deployment

  • Runtime – Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime orchestrates the agents.
  • Orchestration – EventBridge → Lambda → AgentCore runtime → Strands Agents.
  • Security – Machine‑to‑machine credentials (AgentCore Identity) and Amazon Cognito; least‑privilege IAM.
  • Scalability – Each agent runs independently; the architecture supports event‑driven, serverless scaling.

💡 Why it Matters

  • Reduces the manual effort of document processing, freeing up to 30 % of employee time.
  • Cuts error rates by eliminating repetitive extraction failures.
  • Removes the need for constant template maintenance when vendor layouts change.
  • Lowers operational costs for organisations handling hundreds of document sources.
  • Provides a reusable, self‑learning pipeline that improves with every processed document.

#IDP #AmazonBedrock #AIagents #DocumentAutomation

Source: Build self-improving document processing using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services Source: Generate presentations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services Source: How Tamnoon built AI-powered cloud security remediation with Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Google Gemini 4 Argon Model Reaches General Availability with Benchmarks
item.description:
Google Gemini 4 Argon Model Reaches General Availability with Benchmarks

Google announced that Gemini 4 Argon is now generally available (GA) for coding, knowledge work, enterprise workflows and cyber‑defense.

🔍 Overview

  • Gemini 4 Argon went GA today, after a title story was published two weeks earlier.
  • Independent benchmarks such as CursorBench confirm the claims made in the original announcement.
  • The rollout supersedes an earlier claim that access was limited to cybersecurity defenders.

⚙️ Availability

  • Access is provided through the paid Gemini API and Gemini platform.
  • Included in Google AI Pro and Ultra within the Gemini app.
  • Available via AI Mode in Google Search.
  • Ultra model is also accessible in the Antigravity environment.
  • Argon is integrated into third‑party coding tools: Cursor, Devin Desktop/CLI, and GitHub Copilot.
  • Antigravity’s coding interface is entering the Gemini macOS app.
  • Gemini now supports connections to more than 40 applications, including Instacart, OpenTable, Adobe and Shopify.

💰 Pricing

  • Introductory API rates: $2 per million input tokens, $10 per million output tokens.
  • Cached input tokens receive a 95 % discount.
  • Artificial Analysis reports that rates will double to $4/$20 after November 30.
  • Under introductory pricing, Artificial Analysis estimates a cost of $1.99 per task, about 60 % of GPT‑6 Astra’s cost per task.

📊 Benchmarks & Performance

  • CursorBench: Argon scores 52.8 % at default effort, matching Opus 5.5.
  • FrontierCode 1.1: Cognition reports a 60.5 % score; a 75 % Devin discount is available through October 27.
  • Roboflow Evaluation:
    • Text localization/recognition: 84.7 % (Argon) vs 76.8 % (Astra).
    • Object detection: 85.1 % (Argon) vs 83.6 % (Astra).
    • Cost and latency are roughly four times lower, with 19.6 s per image vs 29.7 s for Astra.
  • Arena Ranking: Argon High places fifth behind Opus 5.5, GPT‑6.1 Sol, Fable 5.1 and GPT‑6 Astra at maximum effort.
  • Artificial Analysis: Argon shows substantial agentic gains and a 15 % AA‑Omniscience hallucination rate, the lowest among models scoring ≥45 on the Intelligence Index.
  • DeepMind Robotics Test: Argon derived a cornhole simulation from human video, performed system identification, refined throws on Apptronik’s Apollo robot, and achieved seven consecutive successful throws.
  • LlamaIndex Findings: Argon, Muse Spark and Wonder perform strongly on hard‑document OCR, especially table understanding, chart reading‑order and formatting recognition.

🚀 Use Cases

  • Google reports Argon helped separate core webpage handling from a six‑million‑line legacy Chromium folder, completing months of work in weeks and eliminating a category of browser crashes.
  • Code generation shows a 35 % increase in agentic submissions and a nearly one‑third reduction in rollbacks.
  • The model is being used for OCR tasks, object detection, and robotic control simulations.
  • Integration with over 40 productivity apps expands its reach in enterprise workflows.

📅 Event Coverage

  • About 20,000 attendees joined AIE NYC, where keynotes covered AI × finance, including Anthropic’s AI financial services stack, Vals AI’s benchmarking principles for Argon, and Coatue’s AI‑driven investment decisions.
  • All keynotes are transcribed and talks/workshops will be released as soon as possible.

#Gemini #AIModels #Benchmarking #CodingAI #EnterpriseAI

Source: [AINews] AI Engineer NYC: Gemini 4 Argon, Vals AI Benchmarks

item.title: Guide to Building Production AI Memory Systems
item.description:
Guide to Building Production AI Memory Systems

AI language models are stateless, so every request starts from a blank slate. What feels like memory in a chat window is actually an application trick that resends earlier messages. To give assistants persistent, user‑specific knowledge, developers add a separate engineering layer called an AI memory system. This guide explains the components, workflow, and practical considerations for deploying such a system in production.

🔍 Overview

  • Definition – An AI memory system is a storage and retrieval layer that lets an AI application save useful information, retrieve the relevant parts later, and use them to improve future responses.
  • Stateless models – Large language models are stateless by design; every request receives a prompt, produces a completion, and retains nothing. This is true of GPT‑style models, Claude, Gemini, and open‑source models such as Llama and Mistral alike.
  • Illusion of chat memory – What looks like memory in a chat window is an illusion produced by the application, which resends the earlier messages with each new request. That approach hits a hard ceiling because context windows are finite, long prompts cost more and respond slower, and models tend to use information in the middle of a very long context less reliably than information at the edges.

🧩 How it works

The core of every memory system follows a six‑step pipeline:

Step Description
Capture After each interaction, an extractor decides whether anything is worth keeping and rewrites it as a clean, self‑contained statement (e.g., “Prefers deployment on AWS.”).
Store The statement and its metadata (user ID, timestamp, source, confidence) are stored in a vector database.
Index An embedding model converts the text into a vector, placing similar meanings close together.
Retrieve At query time the system looks for the closest matches, then re‑ranks them by relevance, recency, and importance.
Inject The top memories are formatted into the prompt within a strict token budget.
Generate The language model generates a response using the injected memories; the memory lives in the prompt for minutes and is limited by the context window.

⚙️ Key details

  • External decision making – The memory system decides what to save, where to keep it, and what to place in front of the model on each turn.
  • Memory types –
    • Episodic memory lets an agent learn from experience rather than start over each time.
    • Distilled facts and domain knowledge such as “the user writes Python” or “refunds are allowed within 30 days.”
  • Memory updates – New facts are compared with old ones; duplicates are merged, contradictions are resolved, and stale items are expired.
  • Production definition – A governed data service with write policies, retrieval quality metrics, expiration rules, access controls, and user‑facing edit and delete tools.

💡 Why it matters

  • Without a memory system, developers must rely on ever‑growing prompts, which incur higher costs, slower responses, and reduced reliability of information deep inside the context.
  • An external memory can persist for months or years, enabling assistants to adapt to individual users over long periods.
  • Adding a memory layer transforms a stateless language model into an assistant that remembers preferences, policies, and domain facts across sessions.

#AImemory #LLM #ProductionAI

Source: AI Memory Systems: The Practical Guide to Architecture and Real-World Examples - Dealon.ai

item.title: LFM2.5-24B-A2B: A Fast On-Device MoE Reasoning Model for Agentic Tasks
item.description:
LFM2.5-24B-A2B: A Fast On-Device MoE Reasoning Model for Agentic Tasks

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a new reasoning-only model designed for fast, private agentic workflows on-device. Building upon the LFM2-24B-A2B architecture, this update introduces scaled training, expanded context windows, and explicit chain-of-thought reasoning to provide competitive performance against significantly larger models.

🔍 Overview

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a Mixture of Experts (MoE) model that always produces an explicit chain of thought before providing a final answer. While it is the smallest model in its evaluation group, it is competitive with models like Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, which has ~50% more total and active parameters. Its primary strengths are tool use and instruction following.

🧩 How it works

The model retains its predecessor’s architecture while scaling training and context capabilities:

  • Architecture: 40 layers with 64 experts per MoE block and top-4 routing.
  • Hybrid Design: Uses a combination of gated short convolutions and Grouped Query Attention (GQA).
  • Training Scale: Pre-training was scaled from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training added 2.3T tokens across 32K and 131K context lengths, emphasizing reasoning, math, and long-context data.
  • Tokenizer: An in-place expansion doubled the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for improved non-Latin tokenization.

⚙️ Key details

Feature Specification
Total Parameters 24 Billion
Active Parameters 2 Billion per token
Context Window 131,000 tokens
Vocabulary Size 128,000 tokens

In benchmark testing, the model leads or matches competition on five of eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks. On LiveClaw, it scored 48.09 compared to 38.19 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. On AutomationBench, it scored more than three times the next-best model.

🚀 Availability

LFM2.5-24B-A2B includes day-one support for several inference ecosystems:

  • llama.cpp
  • MLX
  • vLLM
  • SGLang
  • ONNX

💡 Why it matters

This model is optimized for high-speed edge and GPU inference. It decodes at 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395, making it up to 1.7x faster than the next-best compared model while using the least memory. On a single NVIDIA B300 GPU, it can reach over 21,000 output tokens per second. For knowledge-heavy workloads, users are encouraged to pair the model with retrieval or web search, as larger models maintain an edge on benchmarks like GPQA Diamond and SWE-Bench.

#AIagents #EdgeAI #MoE #LiquidFoundationModel

Source: Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

item.title: Shopify Expands Catalog Access to AI Agents for Automated Shopping and Checkout
item.description:
Shopify Expands Catalog Access to AI Agents for Automated Shopping and Checkout

Shopify announced Tuesday it will allow shoppers to configure AI agents to purchase products on their behalf, giving these agents access to a catalog of over a billion listings. This development marks an expansion of the company’s agentic commerce ambitions, moving beyond a previous exclusive partnership with Meta’s Muse agent. Users can now utilize any AI agent for browsing and purchasing without a specific partnership integration.

🔍 Overview

Shopify is marketing the new feature as a “personal shopper” that can act on a human’s behalf. The agent has access to a catalog consisting of items located both on and off Shopify storefronts. This move follows an earlier partnership announced in September with Meta to allow the Muse agent to browse and purchase items.

🧩 How it works

To enable automated shopping, customers must connect an AI agent to their account on Shop, a Shopify-owned platform designed to consolidate orders and track packages.

  • Integration: The agent connects directly to the user’s Shop account.
  • Checkout: Transactions occur via the one-click Shop Pay feature within the conversation with the agent.
  • Order Management: Any orders placed by the agent are funneled back to the Shop app for tracking.

⚙️ Key details

Humans remain in control of the agent’s behavior through specific rules and required authorizations:

  • Budget Guardrails: Users can set spending limits for the agent.
  • Shipping Preferences: Users can instruct agents to only display products with fast shipping.
  • Purchase Approval: Buyers are required to approve each purchase before it is finalized.

💡 Why it matters

E-commerce has emerged as a significant battleground for AI development, with companies like Google and Amazon also investing in tools where the end goal is an autonomous agent purchasing items for users. This shift has also sparked conflict between major commerce players and AI companies, such as the ongoing dispute between Amazon and firms like Perplexity and Meta over whether agents should be permitted to shop on a customer’s behalf.

#Shopify #AIagents #ECommerce #ShopPay #AgenticCommerce

Source: Shopify opens its catalog up to more AI agents

item.title: Orca Security Deploys Discovery AI on AWS Bedrock to Simplify Cloud Queries
item.description:
Orca Security Deploys Discovery AI on AWS Bedrock to Simplify Cloud Queries

Orca Security has released an update to its Discovery AI service, a natural‑language query agent built on Amazon Bedrock that translates plain‑English questions into Sonar queries for its cloud‑security data graph.

🔍 Overview

  • Security analysts need fast answers about their cloud infrastructure without deep familiarity with domain‑specific query languages.
  • Orca Security’s Sonar system tracks more than 900 cloud resource models (e.g., Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon S3 buckets) and requires JSON queries that specify exact model names, select from 18 operators, and navigate parent‑child hierarchies.
  • The original proof‑of‑concept loaded the full Sonar schema (over 900 model definitions) into a single prompt, yielding strong output but high token consumption (~2 million input tokens per workload), high latency (~60 seconds), and limited accuracy on complex multi‑model queries.
  • To address these issues, Orca partnered with AWS to build Discovery AI, a hybrid Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) solution on Amazon Bedrock that converts natural language into validated Discovery filters.

🧩 How It Works

Discovery AI follows a nine‑step pipeline, matching each stage to the most suitable Bedrock model:

  1. Request Entry and Context Setup – Combines the user’s question with organization, connected cloud providers, and request metadata.
  2. Quick Deterministic Matcher – Uses regex and rule‑based matching to detect high‑confidence patterns such as IP addresses, CVEs, ARNs, file hashes, AMI IDs, Oracle Cloud identifiers, EC2 IDs, URLs, and alert IDs.
  3. Fast‑Path Return – When a deterministic match is found, a predefined Discovery filter is returned without invoking an LLM.
  4. (Subsequent stages) – For unmatched requests, the pipeline proceeds through retrieval, schema‑aware construction, and LLM inference stages to produce a Sonar‑compatible JSON query.

Key design choices:

  • Amazon Bedrock provides access to multiple foundation models through a single API, allowing the team to allocate different models to each pipeline stage without separate integrations.
  • Bedrock inherits AWS governance controls (IAM, VPC endpoints, CloudTrail), satisfying Orca’s security requirements.
  • The model‑agnostic architecture enables swapping newer model versions without re‑architecting the pipeline.

⚙️ Key Results

  • Query costs reduced by 90 % compared with the baseline.
  • Input token usage reduced by 93 %.
  • End‑to‑end latency reduced by 75 %, achieving ~15‑second response times (down from ~60 seconds).
  • The system now handles thousands of queries per day.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Analysts can obtain answers without knowing Sonar’s exact schema or the 18‑operator query language.
  • Lower costs and faster responses make continuous cloud‑security monitoring more practical.
  • The hybrid RAG approach demonstrates how Retrieval‑Augmented Generation can be combined with domain‑specific schemas to improve accuracy on complex multi‑model queries.

#OrcaSecurity #AmazonBedrock #DiscoveryAI #CloudSecurity

Source: Natural language security queries at Orca Security using Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Atomic Agent Adds Snowflake Integration via Composio and MCP
item.description:
Atomic Agent Adds Snowflake Integration via Composio and MCP

Atomic Agent, the open‑source on‑device AI assistant, now supports direct interaction with Snowflake through the Composio integration and the Snowflake Model Context Protocol (MCP).

🔍 Overview

  • Atomic Agent runs on your machine and supports local models via llama.cpp.
  • Through Composio it can connect to 1,500+ apps, including Snowflake.
  • Users can issue natural‑language requests such as “list today’s new users” or “cancel a long‑running data import”; authentication is handled automatically.

🧩 How it works

  • Atomic Agent connects to Composio’s Tool Router over Streamable HTTP MCP.
  • For each request the agent discovers the appropriate tools; Composio supplies the necessary account authentication.
  • Execution and account‑connection tools obey the agent’s configured approval policy – you must review any approval prompt before the action proceeds.

⚙️ Setup & Usage

  • Requirements: Atomic Agent v0.5.6 or later, a Composio API key, and a Snowflake account.
  • Add the line below to ~/.atomic‑agent/.env, replacing the placeholder with your key, then start Atomic Agent: 
    1

    COMPOSIO_API_KEY=YOUR_COMPOSIO_API_KEY
  • In Atomic Agent, open the Integrations tab, select Composio, press e, paste the API key, and press Enter. The tools become available immediately, without a restart.
  • Ask Atomic Agent to perform an action in Snowflake. The agent searches Composio for the correct tool. On first use, a sign‑in link is returned in the chat – follow it to connect your Snowflake account, then return to Atomic Agent to continue.

🚀 Availability

  • The Hobby plan includes 100,000 tool calls per month.
  • Integration can be disabled by setting "composio": { "enabled": false } in the config; the saved key remains on disk.

📋 Tool Reference

Tool What it does
Cancel Statement Execution Cancels the execution of a running SQL statement

The Snowflake MCP server implements the Model Context Protocol, giving the agent structured and secure access to the data warehouse and service status. It enables the agent to execute SQL, explore databases and tables, track or cancel statements, inspect catalog integrations, and monitor incidents and maintenance on your behalf.

#AtomicAgent #Snowflake #Composio #AIAgents #MCP

Source: Snowflake MCP Integration with Atomic Agent | Composio

item.title: Claw Code: Rust‑Based Agent‑Managed Museum Exhibit Using Gajae‑Code and LazyCodex
item.description:
Claw Code: Rust‑Based Agent‑Managed Museum Exhibit Using Gajae‑Code and LazyCodex

An agent-managed museum exhibit called Claw Code has been released. It is a public Rust implementation of the claw CLI agent harness, built with the Gajae-Code and LazyCodex toolchains and designed to run without any human intervention.

🔍 Overview

  • The repository is described as a museum exhibit rather than a commercial product.
  • It is “closer to a museum exhibit than a product pitch,” kept alive by “crab‑run” artifact processes and automatically maintained by agents.
  • The project philosophy explicitly states it is not meant to be hand‑operated like a normal product repo.

🛠️ How It Works

  • The exhibit is agent‑managed: harnesses plan, execute, verify, label, and preserve the artifact while “crabs keep the tank running.”
  • The canonical source lives in the rust/ directory, with the current source of truth being ultraworkers/claw-code.
  • claw is the CLI agent harness; Claw Code provides its public Rust implementation.

📦 Getting Started

  • Start with LazyCodex or Gajae‑Code if you want to run work.
  • For build, authentication, CLI usage, session handling, and parity‑harness workflows, consult USAGE.md.
  • After building, run claw doctor as the first health check.
  • Detailed crate information is in rust/README.md; the Rust‑port checkpoint is documented in PARITY.md.
  • Container‑first workflow instructions are in docs/container.md.
  • Windows users can follow the PowerShell‑first quickstart in docs/windows-install-release.md.
  • For file submission or navigation questions, see docs/navigation-file-context.md.
  • Setup for local OpenAI‑compatible models and offline skill installs is covered in docs/local-openai-compatible-providers.md.

📡 Integration & Status

  • ACP / Zed: Claw Code does not ship an ACP/Zed daemon or JSON‑RPC entrypoint yet.
  • Use claw acp (or claw --acp) to query the current status; claw acp serve is a discoverability alias that returns status with exit code 0.
  • Real ACP support remains tracked in ROADMAP.md.
  • The public JSON contract is defined in docs/g011-acp-json-rpc-status-contract.md.

🚀 Availability & Community

  • Repository: ultraworkers/claw-code (GitHub).
  • Join the development discussion on Discord:
    • Harness Lab – Discord‑join the harness lab

item.title: Agenti Gives AI Agents Autonomous Crypto Wallets
item.description:
Agenti Gives AI Agents Autonomous Crypto Wallets

A new development called Agenti lets any AI agent hold, spend, earn, and receive cryptocurrency on its own, removing the need for human‑mediated payments.

🔍 Overview

Agenti provides a crypto wallet that is owned by the AI agent rather than a human, enabling the agent to be funded by its own work, pay for resources, and earn yield when idle.

🧩 How it works

  • A fresh wallet can be generated for both EVM and Solana chains in a single call, or an existing wallet can be loaded. 
  • When an API returns a 402 response, Agenti automatically pays the fee and retries the request. 
  • The @agenti/mcp package turns every SDK tool into an MCP tool that any LLM client can invoke without writing code. 
  • Once configured, you can instruct any LLM with a prompt such as “Pay for this API and summarize the response” and the agent will handle the payment and the task.

⚙️ Key details

  • Supported LLMs – Claude, GPT‑4, Llama, Gemini, or any custom model.
  • Supported chains – EVM and Solana.
  • Compatible clients – Works with Claude, LangChain, AutoGen, CrewAI, and any MCP client.
  • Payment flow – Pay x402 APIs, receive USDC, and check balances autonomously.
  • Ownership – The wallet is owned by the agent, not managed by a human.
  • Economic autonomy – Agents can fund their own operations, compensate other agents, and earn yield.
Component Supported
LLMs Claude, GPT‑4, Llama, Gemini, any custom LLM
Chains EVM, Solana
Clients Claude, LangChain, AutoGen, CrewAI, any MCP client

🚀 Availability

  • The service is hosted at the domain agenti.cash.
  • The project is not published on npm yet; the @agenti scope returns 404 errors (tracked in issue #126).
  • Until the first release is tagged, developers can use the repository directly.
  • The @agenti/mcp package enables MCP‑style tool calls without additional code.

💡 Why it matters

  • Currently, a human must intervene whenever an AI needs to pay for an API, buy a resource, compensate another agent, or receive payment for its work, which breaks autonomy.
  • By giving agents their own wallet, Agenti removes that bottleneck, allowing agents to operate financially independent of humans.
  • The mission expressed in the name—Agenti—is to equip every AI with the ability to manage money autonomously.

#AIAgents #CryptoWallet #AutonomousAI #Blockchain

Source: nirholas/agenti

item.title: Local AI Agent Hermes Enables Personal Automation on High‑Memory Macs
item.description:
Local AI Agent Hermes Enables Personal Automation on High‑Memory Macs

I’m embarking on a journey I’ve so far been hesitant to go on: actually using AI on the regular, this time by running a self‑hosted agent locally on a powerful Mac.

🔍 Overview

  • Concerns about giving personal data to cloud services motivated a shift to local AI.
  • Apple’s new Mac desktops are marketed for local AI workloads, and upcoming RTX Spark Windows machines promise up to 128 GB RAM for agentic AI.
  • The author’s M5 Ultra Mac Studio has 256 GB unified memory, sufficient for almost any model.

🛠️ How it works

  • Hermes is a self‑hosted AI agent desktop app that runs on macOS, Windows, and Linux.
  • It is completely free when using local LLMs.
  • The onboarding interface includes a model picker; the author selected Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, a 125‑billion‑parameter model (~105 GB).
  • Hermes can be controlled via a Telegram bot, enabling daily briefings and other tasks.

📦 Devices & Models

Device Memory / Specs Planned Use
M5 Ultra Mac Studio 256 GB unified memory Run Qwen 3.8 Flash Next and other large models
M6 Mac Mini – Try smaller Qwen models
M5 MacBook Air – Try smaller Qwen models
Asus TUF Gaming A14 (AMD Strix Halo) – Try smaller Qwen models
RTX Spark (future) up to 128 GB RAM Agentic AI experiments

✅ Practical Use Cases

  • Daily morning briefing: Hermes scans email and calendar, reports urgent items and weather; set up as a cron job at 7:30 am (macOS must be awake).
  • Steam library organization: After registering a Steam Web API key, Hermes categorized over 400 games in minutes; the key was revoked afterward.
  • Financial record crunching: Hermes processed sensitive financial data locally.
  • Spec‑comparison spreadsheet: Generated a laptop comparison sheet for a new, embargoed device, keeping the information on‑device.
  • Benchmark automation: Working on a script to run repeated laptop benchmark tests, reducing manual effort.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Local AI requires explicit permissions (e.g., Steam API key) that can be revoked after use.
  • Running models locally eliminates token costs; the author chose a large model to start.
  • Larger models (billions of parameters) generally outperform smaller ones.
  • The daily briefing initially failed until the author ensured the Mac was not asleep when the cron job fired.

💡 Why it matters

  • Sensitive data stays on the user’s machine, addressing privacy concerns with cloud services.
  • Free, local execution of powerful LLMs makes advanced AI capabilities accessible without recurring token fees.
  • A single self‑hosted app can automate a range of personal productivity tasks, from email summaries to game library management.

#LocalAI #Hermes #SelfHosted #LLM #Automation

item.title: TikTok Connects Ads Manager with External AI Agents via MCP Server
item.description:
TikTok Connects Ads Manager with External AI Agents via MCP Server

TikTok has expanded access to its TikTok for Business Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server, allowing advertisers to manage advertising campaigns directly from external AI tools.

🔍 Overview

The TikTok Ads MCP Server connects AI agents and external applications with TikTok Ads features, letting advertisers carry out advertising tasks without jumping into Ads Manager. Originally introduced on May 13, 2026, TikTok announced on October 5, 2026, that the server is available as a connector across several external platforms.

According to TikTok internal data, usage of the MCP server to activate and manage campaigns grew by over 200% between July and September 2026. However, TikTok did not disclose absolute volume, public methodology, or independent verification for this metric.

🧩 How it works

The integration allows advertisers to plan, launch, and manage campaigns through conversational AI interfaces from third-party tools.

  • Authentication: Prebuilt integrations eliminate the need for developer credentials, API keys, and custom code. Connections use OAuth authorization and tokens with the mcp:tt4b permission.
  • Operational Modes: The TikTok for Business help centre outlines two modes:
    • Full mode: Preloaded with around 400 tools.
    • Progressive mode: Starts with roughly 40 tools and discovers new functions as needed.

⚙️ Platform integrations and capabilities

The technical documentation supports the following advertising tasks:

  • Campaign creation
  • Reporting
  • Audience configuration
  • Targeting updates
  • Budget adjustments
  • Pausing ad groups
Platform / Connector Category
Claude AI Platform
Kimi AI Platform
Manus AI Platform
Perplexity AI Platform
Replit AI Platform
Snowflake Data / AI Platform
Tencent WorkBuddy AI Work Platform
IAB Tech Lab agent registry Agent Registry

🚀 Availability

  • Eligibility: Advertisers.
  • Geographic Coverage: Official sources do not confirm availability in Spain or the European Union.
  • Rollout Phase: TikTok has not published a geographic list or formally defined the rollout phase as beta, preview, or general availability.

💡 Controls and recommendations

While the TikTok for Business MCP cuts manual steps, it does not replace account permissions, controls, or human judgment. Granting an AI agent full authority to modify budgets, targeting, or campaign status without approval introduces risks.

Recommended practices include:

  • Establishing permissions, spend limits, change logs, and approval workflows before automating.
  • Testing the MCP server in a controlled account using queries and reports first.
  • Verifying real account access and market availability directly rather than relying solely on announcements.

#TikTok #AIAgents #DigitalAdvertising #ModelContextProtocol #Automation

Source: TikTok for Business MCP: AI-Powered Ad Management

item.title: Anthropic Updates Claude Code with Performance Optimizations and Specialized Agent Skills
item.description:
Anthropic Updates Claude Code with Performance Optimizations and Specialized Agent Skills

Claude Code is an agentic coding tool that lives in the terminal, providing developers with the ability to understand codebases, explain complex logic, and handle git workflows through natural language. The tool has received updates focused on performance optimization, specialized creative skills, and secure execution environments.

🔍 Overview

Claude Code is designed to execute routine tasks and manage codebases with an approach where “the best code is the code you never wrote.” The system is built to make AI agents operate with high efficiency, similar to an experienced senior developer.

  • Terminal-based Operation: Lives directly in the command line for seamless workflow integration.
  • Codebase Understanding: Analyzes and explains complex code structures.
  • Task Execution: Handles routine development tasks and git operations using natural language commands.
  • Core Development: Features a research-first approach incorporating skills, instincts, memory, and security.

⚙️ Key details

The development of Claude Code and related agents now includes specialized skills for both quality control and content production.

  • Taste-Skill: This feature gives the AI “good taste,” stopping it from generating boring or generic content.
  • AI Video Skill: Designed for Claude Code and Codex, this skill enables the creation of cinematic product videos using Remotion. It includes a production-ready template, 152 shot recipe cards, and 209 motion previews.
  • Agent Harness: A performance optimization system designed for Claude Code, Codex, Opencode, and Cursor.

🧩 How it works

The system utilizes a hybrid architecture to ensure precise code analysis and secure execution.

  • Hybrid Code Review: Combines deterministic pipelines with LLM Agents to deliver precise, line-level comments. It includes built-in rulesets for multiple languages to detect Null Pointer Exceptions (NPE), thread-safety issues, XSS, and SQL injection.
  • OpenShell Runtime: Provides a safe and private runtime environment specifically for autonomous AI agents.
  • Model Compatibility: Supports cross-converting various models into OpenAI, Claude, or Gemini-compatible formats through a unified hub.

🛠️ Infrastructure and Access

Component Description
OpenClaw An agent-first Identity and Access Management (IAM) and auth server supporting OAuth, OIDC, and MFA.
Sub2API A unified open-source service for accessing Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, and Grok subscriptions.
OpenShell A safe, private runtime environment for autonomous agents.

item.title: China Telecom’s TeleAgent reaches 1.5 million users and launches private‑deployment edition
item.description:
China Telecom’s TeleAgent reaches 1.5 million users and launches private‑deployment edition

China Telecom’s office AI agent, TeleAgent, announced that it has grown to 1.5 million registered users and over 200,000 daily active users – a sharp rise from just 27,000 registered users in mid‑June. The milestone was revealed by Liu Guiqing at the opening of PT Expo China 2026, after the product’s first unveiling at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC) 2026.

🔍 Overview

  • User growth: 1.5 M registered users, >200 K DAU (up from 27 K in mid‑June).\
  • Announcement: Liu Guiqing, Executive Director, President and COO of China Telecommunications Corporation, at PT Expo China 2026.\
  • First reveal: WAIC 2026.

🧩 How it works

  • Built by China Telecom AI Technology Co. (TeleAI) as a native workplace AI application.
  • Runs natively on Windows, macOS, Kylin OS and UnionTech OS (UOS) – no complex server setup needed for individual users.
  • Users simply drag and drop files into the workspace; the agent executes end‑to‑end tasks.
  • Leverages China Telecom’s Xingchen multimodal foundation model and the “five‑in‑one” intelligent cloud.
  • Implements “Token‑based operations”: an intelligent model router selects the most cost‑effective foundation model and uses context compression to lower latency and inference costs.
  • Persistent long‑term memory adapts to user habits over time.

⚙️ Key details

Edition Core Feature
Enterprise SaaS Multi‑device collaboration and scenario customisation
Private‑deployment (released mid‑August) Models and data remain entirely within the customer’s local, sovereign environment
  • Skill marketplace grew from ~40 K to >50 K skills; 99 % of skills were created by end users solving real‑world productivity challenges.
  • Supports professionals, SMEs and large state‑owned conglomerates.

🔐 Security

  • Lightweight security sandbox isolates file access.
  • Certifications from the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology (CAICT).
  • Cleared 99.7 % of 336 threat‑evaluation scenarios conducted by QiAnXin and other leading security vendors.

📈 Adoption & Impact

    • 90 % say the agent is integral to daily routines.

item.title: Microsoft Agent Framework succeeds AutoGen as repository enters maintenance mode
item.description:
Microsoft Agent Framework succeeds AutoGen as repository enters maintenance mode

AutoGen’s repository has officially transitioned into maintenance mode, receiving no new features or enhancements as it moves to a community-managed model. Microsoft is directing new users to the Microsoft Agent Framework, a .NET and Python framework for agents and multi-agent workflows, and has provided a migration guide for current AutoGen users.

🧩 How it works

AutoGen enables the creation of agents that interact within a shared conversation. This framework is built for asynchronous operation, utilizing an AgentChat API where developers write async def functions and execute them with asyncio.run. To avoid resource leaks, developers must ensure they call await model_client.close() to release LLM connections.

A typical implementation might involve a writer drafting content and a critic responding to the draft. In this setup, the critic views the draft cold, with no investment in defending the work, and the loop continues until a termination condition is triggered.

⚙️ Key details

Termination conditions are the primary safety feature for agent teams, preventing agents from infinitely exchanging messages and incurring unnecessary costs. The framework allows developers to join conditions using the | operator, stopping the run as soon as any single condition fires.

Termination Condition Description
TextMentionTermination("APPROVE") Ends the run when a message contains the specific trigger word.
MaxMessageTermination Acts as a hard cap on the total number of messages in a run.
External Termination An object that can be fired from your application to stop the team.

🚀 Availability

To use the framework, Python 3.10 or later is required. While examples typically utilize the OpenAI API via the OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable, other providers are supported through specific client classes in extension packages. Agents also gain increased utility through the integration of tools.

Developers can execute agent teams in two ways:

  • await team.run(task=...): Returns a TaskResult including a stop reason once the team concludes.
  • team.run_stream(task=...): Yields messages as they arrive, which can be printed using Console during development.

Teams maintain their state between runs. To prevent old context from leaking into new tasks, developers should call await team.reset() before reuse.

#Microsoft #AutoGen #AIAgents #Python #SoftwareDevelopment

Source: AutoGen Tutorial: Multi-Agent Conversations with Microsoft’s Framework | Sam Austin AI

item.title: OpenAI Unveils Dots AI Agent as Privacy-Focused Alternative to Meta Muse
item.description:
OpenAI Unveils Dots AI Agent as Privacy-Focused Alternative to Meta Muse

At this year’s OpenAI DevDay, CEO Sam Altman introduced Dots, a new AI agent designed to set a new standard for privacy in frontier AI. The announcement included direct critiques of Meta’s Muse, with OpenAI positioning its new assistant as a more secure and trustworthy alternative to its primary competitor.

🔍 Overview

OpenAI executives used the launch of Dots to highlight security concerns surrounding Meta’s Muse, which had previously launched as a safer alternative to the agent OpenClaw. While Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg promised Muse was built for privacy and security, the platform has faced scrutiny over data collection and vulnerabilities. OpenAI’s leadership, including Codex product lead Alexander Embiricos, stated the company is focused on providing the most secure assistant while avoiding the mistakes of rivals.

⚙️ Key details

AI Agent Developer Stated Privacy and Security Approach
Dots OpenAI Zero data retention policy options for enterprises and individual user-set rules.
Muse Meta User data stored in isolated Linux VMs with browser, CPU, memory, and storage.
OpenClaw (Not specified) Predecessor to Muse; described as less safe than subsequent alternatives.

🧩 Capabilities and Controls

OpenAI and Meta have implemented different strategies to manage user data and agent behavior:

  • OpenAI Dots: Users can exert individual control over the agent, such as setting rules to prevent it from making purchases over a specific dollar amount. Enterprise customers can access frameworks with stronger data controls and options to ensure no data is stored on OpenAI servers.
  • Meta Muse: The agent defaults to allowing Meta to train models on user input, though an opt-out is available. While the company plans to introduce cryptographic methods to prevent internal access to VM data, Meta currently retains access.

🚀 Availability

OpenAI has launched Dots with a focus on its high-end user base, currently making it available only on the $100-and-up ChatGPT subscription tiers. In contrast, Meta’s Muse saw rapid adoption following its release, gaining 600,000 daily active users in the United States within weeks and topping App Store charts.

💡 Why it matters

The push for more private AI agents comes as labs try to convince users to share increasingly personal information. Despite Meta’s privacy promises for Muse, security researchers exposed a zero-day vulnerability, and reports indicated the agent created detailed profiles of users’ social networks and shared private data, such as physical addresses and private messages, as part of its intended functions. OpenAI’s strategy with Dots relies on one-upping these rivals by promising stricter data boundaries, though some users still report discomfort when asked to provide sensitive financial information to these agents.

#OpenAI #Dots #Meta #AIAgents #DataPrivacy

Source: AI agent makers are promising privacy — will they deliver?

item.title: Agent-Controlled Forgetting Reduces Token Usage for Tool-Using AI Agents
item.description:
Agent-Controlled Forgetting Reduces Token Usage for Tool-Using AI Agents

Researchers introduced a reversible context curation technique called agent‑controlled forgetting for tool‑using language‑model agents.

🔍 Overview

  • Tool‑using agents often retain full tool output even when most of it is irrelevant.
  • Agent‑controlled forgetting replaces each observed tool result with a short note while storing the original in a recoverable archive.

🧩 How it Works

  • The acting model selects previously observed tool results.
  • Each selected result is replaced with a concise note at its original position.
  • The full original is kept in an archive that can be recovered on demand.
  • A Python harness provides batch archival and explicit recovery, requires no task‑specific model training, and protects user instructions and assistant messages from these operations.

📊 Results

  • In an OpenTelemetry debugging case followed by an unrelated implementation task:
    • Provider‑reported prompt tokens: 231,951 with forgetting vs 912,492 with retained history.
    • Cumulative input tokens reduced by roughly 50 %.
    • Estimated API cost: $1.28‑$1.44 versus approximately $4.38.
  • Both experimental arms passed the two‑case primary behavioral oracle; neither fully satisfied the follow‑up evaluation.
  • The forgetting method made more API requests and took 17 % longer.
  • A contrasting application‑development pair showed no context or cost saving, and an earlier continuation exhibited lower manually assessed quality despite reduced context.

⚠️ Limitations & Workload Dependence

  • Resource savings are substantial in noisy tool‑use trajectories but depend on the workload.
  • The method can increase request count and latency.
  • In some workloads, no context or cost benefit was observed, and quality may decrease.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Demonstrates a practical reversible context management strategy for agents that use external tools.
  • Highlights trade‑offs between token efficiency, latency, and task quality.
  • Suggests that workload characteristics should guide the use of reversible context curation.

#AIagents #contextmanagement #tooluse #LLM #tokenoptimization

Source: Agent-Controlled Forgetting for Tool-Using Agents: Reversible Context Curation in Practice Source: Curating Always-Loaded Context for LLM Agents: A Capacitated Assortment Model with Censored Feedback Source: What to Admit and How to Present: Governing Persistent Memory in LLM Agents Source: MemoWM: How World Models Change What Agents Need to Remember Source: Gated Memory: Admission-Controlled Memory Formation for Conversational AI

item.title: Agentic AI Design Patterns and Visual Workflow Builders Gain Traction in 2026
item.description:
Agentic AI Design Patterns and Visual Workflow Builders Gain Traction in 2026

🔍 Overview

Agentic AI design patterns—reusable blueprints that tell an AI agent how to reason, act, and improve its own work—are becoming the core of production‑grade AI agents. 2026 sees these patterns packaged in frameworks like LangGraph, AutoGen, and CrewAI, while visual workflow builders such as Workflow Builder, Dify, Langflow, n8n, and Sim make the engineering of complex agentic systems easier.

🧩 Core Agentic AI Design Patterns

  • Reflection – the agent drafts output, critiques it against clear criteria, then revises. It adds virtually no cost because it requires no new tools, only an extra pass. Research (Reflexion, Self‑Refine) shows that a weaker model wrapped in a reflection loop can beat a stronger model used zero‑shot.
  • Tool Use – the agent calls APIs, databases, or code to take action (e.g., running tests, reading failures, rewriting code).
  • Planning – the agent breaks a big goal into ordered steps and adapts when a step fails. Two common styles:
    • ReAct interleaves reasoning and action, choosing the next step after each result.
    • Plan‑and‑execute writes the full plan first, runs it, and replans only on failure.
  • Multi‑Agent Collaboration – specialised agents (researcher, coder, reviewer) split work and hand results to each other. Centralised coordination improved results by roughly 81 % on parallelisable tasks in Google Research tests, while poorly designed multi‑agent variants degraded performance by 39‑70 %.

⚙️ Implementations & Frameworks

  • LangGraph, Microsoft AutoGen, CrewAI – ship the four patterns as building blocks. Andrew Ng popularised the framing in 2024, and the same patterns appear in Anthropic’s guide to effective agents.
  • Production advice – combine two or three patterns: a core reasoning or planning loop, tools for action, and reflection for quality. Add multi‑agent setups only when sub‑tasks are genuinely independent. Cap retries at two or three and prefer external signals (unit tests, linters, schema validators) over self‑opinion.
  • Cost and risk – Gartner expects over 40 % of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027 due to rising costs, unclear value, and weak risk controls. The simplest pattern that solves the task is usually the right one.

📊 Choosing Visual Workflow Builders

Builder Primary Strength Ideal Use Case
Workflow Builder Embedded visual editor that lives inside a product Customer‑facing AI products needing an in‑app authoring layer
Dify All‑in‑one platform for building, testing, and deploying AI applications Internal AI products, prototyping, teams wanting a single system for the lifecycle
Langflow Rapid composition of agentic and RAG flows with strong Python ecosystem Python‑based agents and Retrieval‑Augmented Generation workflows
n8n Integration of AI agents with broader business automation Scenarios where agents sit inside existing automation environments
Sim Modern open‑source workspace with visual workflows, deployment, versioning Teams wanting open‑source flexibility and version control
Flowise (Archived) End of life announced August 2026; no longer a live option

Selection tips – Consider who will author the workflows, which system will handle execution, and how much control you need over the user experience and workflow data.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Gartner forecasts that 33 % of enterprise software applications will include agentic AI by 2028, up from under 1 % in 2024.
  • In production, a sound agent architecture (core reasoning/planning + tools + reflection) matters more than the underlying LLM model.
  • Visual workflow builders reduce the engineering burden by letting teams define, inspect, and change agent behavior without turning every adjustment into code.
  • Properly scoped patterns—using reflection for quality, planning for multi‑step tasks, and restrained multi‑agent collaboration—help keep token usage, latency, and cost under control while delivering reliable, testable AI agents.

#AIagents #AgenticAI #WorkflowBuilders #LLM

Source: Agentic AI Design Patterns | 4 Patterns to Know (2026) Source: Workflow Builder - Best visual workflow builders for AI agent applications in 2026 Source: Building Your Own AI Agent Server

item.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Payments Enables Per‑Inference Payments for Autonomous Agents
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Payments Enables Per‑Inference Payments for Autonomous Agents

When an autonomous AI agent needs to buy a service – a model inference, an API response, or web access – those purchases are tiny, frequent, and happen inside the agent’s loop without a human to approve each one. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Payments removes that bottleneck by giving agents a managed, spend‑limit‑enforced way to pay for services on demand.

🔍 Overview

  • Agents often make hundreds of small purchases in a single session, each worth a fraction of a cent.
  • Building a custom payment rail requires solving wallet management, transaction signing, protocol support, and overspend protection.
  • AgentCore Payments provides a managed capability that handles these concerns in just a few lines of code.

🧩 How It Works

  1. AgentCore runs the agent (any framework or model).
  2. BlockRun acts as the seller, providing metered model inference via an x402‑compatible endpoint. Each call is quoted, paid, and settled individually.
  3. AgentCore Payments connects to the agent’s wallet (e.g., a Coinbase CDP‑provisioned wallet) and:
    • Detects an HTTP 402 Payment Required response.
    • Signs the transaction with the configured wallet.
    • Returns cryptographic proof to the merchant.
    • Enforces a spending ceiling set at the infrastructure layer.
  4. Payments settle in a stablecoin (USDC on the Base network) and are verifiable on‑chain.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Managed wallets – Incarna provisions each agent’s wallet via the Coinbase CDP connector.
  • Native protocol handling – AgentCore Payments works with any x402‑compatible endpoint, including Amazon Bedrock inference endpoints.
  • Spending limits – Limits are enforced by the infrastructure, not by the model, preventing overspend.
  • Payment schemes – Supports two x402 schemes: exact and upto; a session sets a ceiling that the agent cannot exceed.
  • Time savings – The Incarna team reduced the effort to add x402 payment support from months to days and launched an end‑to‑end pay‑per‑inference flow in production.
  • Integration steps – Use the AgentCore payments skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS to store payment credentials (Coinbase CDP or Stripe Privy) in AWS Secrets Manager, create a Payment Manager, and set a default spending limit.

🚀 Availability

AgentCore Payments is a managed capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and can be enabled through a guided conversation with the AgentCore payments skill. It works with any framework or model that can call x402‑compatible endpoints.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Automation at scale – Enables autonomous agents to purchase needed services without human intervention.
  • Financial control – Infrastructure‑level spending caps protect budgets while allowing high‑frequency, low‑value transactions.
  • Simplified development – Teams can focus on agent logic instead of building and securing custom payment infrastructure.
  • Auditable transactions – On‑chain settlement in USDC provides transparent, verifiable payment records.

#AmazonBedrock #AIagents #Payments #x402 #Stablecoin

Source: Pay-per-inference for AI agents: How BlockRun and Incarna use Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Amazon Bedrock expands agent capabilities with AgentCore and new frontier models
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock expands agent capabilities with AgentCore and new frontier models

Amazon Bedrock has launched new tools and models designed to simplify the development and deployment of enterprise AI agents. This update includes the introduction of AgentCore for managed infrastructure, the public preview of Managed Agents powered by OpenAI, and the addition of several high-performance models from partners such as Moonshot AI, xAI, and Anthropic. These enhancements focus on providing enterprise security, auditability through AWS CloudTrail, and more efficient memory management for serverless agents.

🔍 Overview

Amazon Bedrock now provides a broader ecosystem for building and connecting AI agents through both managed services and open-source toolkits. Key infrastructure updates include:

  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: Managed infrastructure to build, connect, and deploy agents using any framework or model.
  • Managed Agents: Now in public preview, these OpenAI-powered agents allow users to keep data within AWS while utilizing existing IAM permissions.
  • Strands: An open-source toolkit and harness designed for building agents that can run anywhere with 28 percent fewer tokens than popular alternatives.
  • AgentCore Runtime: Features improved memory management and lower cold start latency, allowing users to pay for actual usage rather than peak memory.

🧩 How it works

Building agents for production environments requires addressing architectural challenges such as tool selection and session management. The new capabilities handle these through hardware-isolated environments and specialized models:

  • Decision Modeling: The Strands Decider 2B is a small, 2B-parameter open-source model that selects between predefined options in approximately 115ms locally, optimizing tasks like tool selection and routing.
  • Session Scaling: Sessions now scale to zero when idle to manage costs.
  • Human Oversight: In production designs like Postman’s Agent Mode, agents require user approval before modifying application state.
  • Security Controls: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can be used to redact personally identifiable information (PII) before data reaches the underlying large language model.

⚙️ Key details

The update introduces a significant variety of new foundation models optimized for different agentic tasks:

Model Key Features
GPT-6 Astra Flagship model with up to 1 million input tokens for complex reasoning
GPT-6 Astra Ultrafast Premium speed tier delivering up to 300 tokens per second
Sol (GPT-6 / 6.1) Designed for coding, computer use, and professional workloads
Luna (GPT-6.1) Optimized for high-volume extraction, summarization, and routing
Claude Opus 5.5 Features adaptive thinking and an effort parameter to bound reasoning depth
Claude Sonnet 5.5 30 percent lower cost and 30 percent faster than Claude Sonnet 5
Kimi K3 First open model with 2.8 trillion parameters and native vision
Grok 4.6 / 4.7 500K token context window with support for self-verification

🚀 Availability

Many of these features and models are available now or in public preview on Amazon Bedrock:

  • Public Preview: Amazon Bedrock Managed Agents powered by OpenAI.
  • General Availability: OpenAI Astra, Sol, and Luna models.
  • New Model Additions: Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Moonshot AI Kimi K3, and xAI Grok 4.6 and 4.7.
  • Open Source: Strands toolkit, Decider 2B model, and agent harness are available on GitHub and Hugging Face.

💡 Why it matters

Moving an agent from a demo to a production environment involves complex engineering, particularly regarding “tool sprawl.” Postman found that tool-selection errors increased once a visible toolset exceeded approximately 40 tools. By using Bedrock’s managed infrastructure, organizations can scale production workloads without operating their own model-serving infrastructure. This allows for geographically scoped cross-Region inference, model-dependent zero data retention, and multi-tier prompt caching to maintain speed and cost efficiency.

#AmazonBedrock #AIagents #OpenAI #CloudComputing #GenerativeAI

Source: ICYMI: What landed for AI builders in September 2026 | Amazon Web Services Source: How Postman runs Agent Mode for 40 million developers on Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Instinct AI Launches Text-Based Assistant With 10 Billion Dollar Valuation
item.description:
Instinct AI Launches Text-Based Assistant With 10 Billion Dollar Valuation

Instinct AI, a startup founded by former Sierra employee Noah Shinn, has launched a new AI agent that operates through a straightforward text message interface. After a quiet release in August that relied on an invite-only model with no marketing, the company was valued at $10 billion in late September, despite mounting pressure from competitors like OpenAI and Meta.

🔍 Overview

Instinct is designed as a consumer-friendly AI agent that handles personal chores and administrative tasks. Unlike many contemporary AI products that use traditional app interfaces or anthropomorphized mascots, Instinct operates entirely through existing messaging channels. The startup focuses on a specific niche that founder Noah Shinn believes sets it apart from larger players building products for a broader range of customers.

🧩 How it works

Instinct functions by providing the AI assistant with access to a virtual machine and personal integrations.

  • Interface: Conversations happen exclusively over text through iMessage, WhatsApp, or email.
  • Integrations: Users can connect the agent to Google Workspace, Slack, and Notion.
  • Security: To log into specific websites, the agent provides a link to a “secure vault” where users enter their credentials.
  • System Access: The agent can plug directly into a user’s personal email and calendar to manage schedules.

⚙️ Key details

The agent is a consumer-oriented version of developer tools like Codex and OpenClaw. It is capable of handling vague instructions and managing various digital tasks:

Task Type Examples of Capabilities
Appointments Booking DMV appointments and emailing doctor’s offices to set up visits.
Communications Sending follow-up emails and handling digital paperwork for Ikea returns.
Research Finding age-appropriate lessons and verifying times and dates for community center classes.

🚀 Availability

Instinct currently lacks a traditional app or a monthly subscription fee. Access is limited through the following methods:

  • An invitation from a current user.
  • Approval from a waitlist.

Because it relies on text messaging, the service is accessible on any device that supports iMessage or WhatsApp, including CarPlay and smartwatches.

💡 Why it matters

The launch of Instinct represents a shift toward autonomous agents for the general public. While the agent has demonstrated some limitations—such as missing specific prerequisite information for class enrollments—its ability to operate across various messaging platforms without a dedicated app separates it from the “cuddly bear” or “blob” mascots used by competitors like Muse and Dots. Shinn remains unfazed by the competition, citing Instinct’s specialized focus as its primary advantage.

#InstinctAI #AIAgents #Startups #OpenAI #NoahShinn

item.title: LLM-IDEA Proposed to Resolve Identifiability Plateaus in Autonomous Scientific Discovery
item.description:
LLM-IDEA Proposed to Resolve Identifiability Plateaus in Autonomous Scientific Discovery

Submitted on October 8, 2026, a new development introduces the Identifiability-Driven Experimental Agent (LLM-IDEA) to address the issue of model identifiability in autonomous scientific discovery. While large language model agents are increasingly deployed as autonomous scientists to design experiments and infer mechanistic world models with minimal human oversight, they often struggle when reaching a plateau because they cannot determine whether they lack capability or if the model simply cannot be identified from the data.

🧩 How it works

LLM-IDEA introduces an identifiability engine that computes a three-way plateau verdict to guide the agent when progress stalls, replacing guesswork with computation. The three verdicts are:

  • Capability limit: The agent is not yet capable enough.
  • Resolvable within the design class: The model can be resolved with further experiments of the same kind.
  • Certified exhausted: No amount of further experimentation of the same kind can help.

📊 System Evaluations

The identifiability engine has been tested across various environments and benchmarks:

System / Benchmark Results and Verdicts
ODEBench 60 of the 62 systems with free constants are identifiable at round 0.
RC Circuit Certified exhausted for every experiment that the protocol can run.
Harvesting Model Resolvable by one added initial condition.
Known Models (Lotka-Volterra, Van der Pol, Lorenz, Pharmacokinetic) The engine reproduces known verdicts. In the pharmacokinetic model, it recommends the intravenous arm that pharmacologists use. It also ranks the depth scorer of the authors’ own benchmark last among four observation designs.
DiscoverPhysics Benchmark Finds two public worlds whose explanation rubric rewards a distinction no legal experiment can make. Every model with accurate trajectories failed the explanation grade (15 of 15, compared to 5 of 9 in identifiable worlds, p = 0.012).
Alien Universe A proposed two-body testbed where a force law switches between a provably non-identifiable and an identifiable protocol. LLM-IDEA on the identifiable protocol reaches a discovery depth of at least three on 8/8 seeds, compared to 1/8 seeds without it.

💡 Why it matters

By computing rather than guessing, an autonomous discovery agent can now determine whether a scientific plateau requires more search, a better experiment of the same kind, or an entirely different kind of experiment.

#AIagents #AutonomousScience #LLM_IDEA #MachineLearning

Source: LLM-IDEA: Identifiability-Driven Experimental Agent for Autonomous Discovery of Mechanistic World Models

item.title: NVIDIA KGMON Team Secures Second Place at KDD Cup 2026 with Agent Harness
item.description:
NVIDIA KGMON Team Secures Second Place at KDD Cup 2026 with Agent Harness

The NVIDIA KGMON team placed second in the KDD Cup 2026 Data Agents competition with a system that streamlines the agent harness to be smaller, clearer, and easier to verify.

🔍 Overview

  • The competition required agents to answer natural‑language questions over heterogeneous data sources such as databases, CSV/JSON files, prose documents, PDFs, and briefing videos.
  • Every task demanded more than simple retrieval: agents had to inspect data, choose appropriate tools, reason across sources, produce a final answer file, and navigate traps common in analytical workflows.
  • Teams were limited to a small, fixed LLM, making the harness the primary optimization surface.
  • KGMON’s approach focused on preprocessing, constrained tools, persistent state, and systematic evaluation to make the task easier for the available model.

🛠️ Architecture & Workflow

  • Unified data access – CSV and JSON files were converted into tables inside a single SQLite database, giving the agent one SQL interface for all structured data.
  • Single tool set – The environment exposed only a few helpers: schema inspection, SQL queries, document lookup, prose extraction, and answer writing.
  • Schema‑scouting step – Before the main reasoning loop the system inspected tables, columns, join keys, duplicate names, units, null patterns, and row‑grain issues, then supplied this context to the agent.
  • Middleware repair – Malformed tool calls were automatically fixed so a single bad call would not abort the attempt.
  • Stateful Python environment – Variables persisted between tool calls, allowing reuse of intermediate results.
  • Predefined functions – schema(), sql(query), and write_answer(df) reduced boilerplate, syntax errors, and file‑handling mistakes.
  • Execution tracing – Repeated attempts and trajectory inspection helped identify failures and refine the harness.
Function / Helper Role
schema() Provide the agent with table and column metadata discovered during scouting
sql(query) Execute a SQL statement against the unified SQLite database
write_answer(df) Write the final answer file in the required format
Document lookup Retrieve relevant prose or PDF content
Prose extraction Pull specific text snippets from unstructured documents

Figure 1 (see below) illustrates the overall workflow from data ingestion to final answer generation.

⚙️ Reliability Techniques

  • Preprocessing data into a uniform SQL schema reduced routing failures and saved turns for reasoning.
  • Constrained tool set limited the ways the agent could interact with the environment, lowering the chance of mistakes.
  • Persistent state and middleware repair prevented a single error from ending an attempt.
  • Short, valid attempts conserved the limited turn budget for additional runs, evaluation, and ensembling.
  • Execution traces and trajectory inspection were used to pinpoint failures such as bad tool calls or answer‑format issues.

🚩 Common Failure Modes

  • Bad tool call (e.g., syntax error)
  • Incorrect join key leading to wrong results
  • Missed document rule or threshold in unstructured sources
  • Answer‑format mismatch causing the final output to be rejected

💡 Why It Matters

  • The techniques are especially useful when building reliable systems around smaller open models.
  • Reliability often stems more from a well‑designed harness than from expanding the openness of the model itself.
  • A streamlined harness leaves more capacity for the fixed LLM to focus on analysis rather than plumbing.

Figure 1: Overall workflow of the KGMON system

#KDD2026 #AIAgents #NVIDIA #LLM #DataIntegration

Source: Building Reliable Data Analytics Agents: Lessons from the KDD Cup | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: Ripwire: Zero‑Dependency C++23 CLI for Multi‑Agent Code Navigation
item.description:
Ripwire: Zero‑Dependency C++23 CLI for Multi‑Agent Code Navigation

The new tool ripwire provides a zero‑dependency C++23 CLI + MCP server for coding agents.

🔍 Overview

  • “Zero‑dependency C++23 CLI + MCP server for coding agents.”
  • “Find what you want without reading the repo, then check you built what you meant — blast radius, tests-to-run, quality deltas.”
  • “Signatures at 74.7% fewer bytes than bodies; every guess labelled, every loss published.”
  • “Ranked, deterministic call graph: what to touch, what it breaks, which tests to run.”
  • “On the edit: blast radius, tests that reach it, eleven quality kinds reporting only what got worse, forgotten co‑changes, fields read and written, names that resolve more than one way.”

🧩 How it works

  • The tool builds a deterministic call graph that tells you what to touch, what it breaks, and which tests to run.
  • It reports blast radius and the set of tests that reach any edit.
  • Signatures are stored at 74.7% fewer bytes than full bodies, with every guess labelled and every loss published.
  • Queries such as --callers and --edit-check surface hidden dependencies and incompatibilities that plain text search would miss.

⚙️ Key details

  • “Whole‑workflow ~2×; per‑lookup 10–25×; and two moments where one call was worth more than the rest of the session’s tooling combined.”
  • “Roughly half the total token spend of the audit/research phase, saved.”
  • “A single doc‑recall call served the relevant sections of a 164KB planning document in ~6K tokens (~25×).”
  • “Agents that led with the tool ran ~30–40% leaner on tool‑call counts than agents doing raw read fan‑outs over comparable questions.”
  • “Two tasks had their direction changed by a single call.”
  • “One --callers query returned zero production callers, redirecting the task to the real gap.”
  • “--edit-check flagged 5 of 6 call sites as incompatible — sites a text search had missed — that would otherwise have silently diverged from the canonical path …”
  • “A dozen‑plus real code‑quality defects fixed, not waived, across ~15 implementing agents — all caught by --quality-delta at each agent’s "I think I’m done" moment.”
  • “Examples include a 480‑token duplicated routine, a fourth private copy of a shared RNG utility, a hand‑duplicated cost function, a pair of near‑identical functions with a flipped sign, test‑fixture duplication across sibling suites, and functions that had quietly absorbed a second job.”
  • “None of these would have failed a test; all of them are the sediment that rots a codebase under high‑velocity multi‑agent development.”
  • “The gate made removing them routine instead of heroic.”

🚀 Availability

  • “Just want to use it? Install it with the one line below, then start each coding session by telling your agent to use it, for example: "Use ripwire on this repo."”
  • “The install also teaches your agent when to reach for each command.”
  • “Want every detail? The reference guide near the bottom covers install, commands, output format, exit codes and limits.”
  • “You do not need it to get started.”

💡 Why it matters

  • For a single developer, the tool is a “good lookup accelerator.”
  • For an orchestrated fleet, it is “load‑bearing: it halved the research spend, twice redirected tasks before wasted work, prevented at least one silent‑divergence shipped bug, and turned code‑quality hygiene from a hope into a per‑task mechanical gate.”
  • The reported field study was written by Claude Fable 5.0, the frontier model orchestrating ~20 coding agents over two days on a ~1,500‑file C++/Metal codebase.

#AIcoding #Ripwire #CodeQuality #MultiAgent

Source: redhat-et/ripwire

item.title: Goldsmith: An Agentic Pipeline for Learning Structured Annotation Definitions
item.description:
Goldsmith: An Agentic Pipeline for Learning Structured Annotation Definitions

Many annotation projects begin before experts have a stable guideline or enough labels to train a task‑specific model.

🔍 Overview

  • Goldsmith is an agentic pipeline that converts a small gold set—expert‑annotated calibration examples that capture the intended task boundaries—into a reusable structured annotation definition.
  • The definition is treated as a trainable textual object.

🧩 How It Works

  • Candidate definitions are executed on the same gold examples and scored with an executable structured loss.
  • Core components such as output schema, formatting, retrieval, repair, judging, and human review stay in an external harness.
  • An LLM editor rewrites the highest‑loss failures into textual‑gradient revisions; revisions are accepted only when the measured loss decreases.

⚙️ Key Results

  • In prompt‑optimization comparisons, Goldsmith outperforms direct rewriting, OPRO, APE, and PromptBreeder when evaluated under matched protocols.
  • When combined with retrieval, score‑based routing, and human review, the learned definition improves downstream annotation for:
    • Typed span tasks
    • Pair‑level relation tasks
    • Fixed‑trigger event‑argument tasks
  • These findings demonstrate that scarce expert supervision can support both task‑definition learning and scalable annotation.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Provides a systematic way to bootstrap annotation pipelines without requiring extensive labeled data up front.
  • Leverages the expressive power of LLMs to iteratively refine task definitions while maintaining a measurable loss signal.
  • Enables more efficient use of expert effort, reducing the barrier to high‑quality annotation for new tasks.

#annotation #LLM #promptoptimization #AItools

Source: Goldsmith: Gold-Loss-Guided Definition Optimization with an Agentic Annotation Harness Source: A Comparative Study of Evaluation Metrics for Long-Document Financial Narrative Summarization with Transformers

item.title: Google Launches Universal Gemini AI Agent for Enterprise Work Tasks

Google Launches Universal Gemini AI Agent for Enterprise Work Tasks

Google has announced a “universal” Gemini AI agent designed to work across apps and devices in the background to handle enterprise work tasks. Revealed during the Gemini at Work event on Thursday, the agent allows users to assign tasks and chat from a single interface within the Gemini Enterprise app.

🧩 How it works

The new Gemini agent is built to streamline workflows by operating across various environments:

  • Smart model selection: Gemini automatically performs tasks using whichever AI model best fits the specific job.
